KEN CARYL, Colo.—A new residential development south of Denver is the testing ground for an unusual partnership that could transform home heating and cooling across the country.
Dandelion Energy, a geothermal startup, and Lennar, one of the nation’s largest homebuilders, recently completed construction of nearly 100 homes at the base of Colorado’s Front Range, each equipped with its own ground-source heat pump. The systems use less electricity than even the most efficient air-source heat pumps, potentially helping Colorado meet its climate goals while reducing peak energy demand and eliminating the need for new gas pipelines.
Ground-source heat pumps draw on steady temperatures belowground to help heat and cool buildings. However, the projects’ custom designs and drilling requirements—homes typically require one or more boreholes drilled several hundred feet deep—are pricey. Drilling alone often costs more than $10,000.
Dandelion, a company that got its start at X—a “moonshot” research and development subsidiary of Alphabet, Google’s parent company—says it can complete geothermal heating and cooling projects twice as fast and at half the cost of similar installations.
The company is “taking a kind of mass market and maximally efficient lens to what has historically been a bespoke kind of custom, high-end product,” said Dan Yates, Dandelion Energy’s CEO and chairman.
Earlier this year at Lennar’s Ken Caryl Ranch development, Dandelion’s drill team demonstrated a lightweight rig designed to quickly move from lot to lot, drilling boreholes and installing polyethylene pipe across the sprawling housing development before building foundations are poured.
Each home gets a single bore between 200 and 500 feet deep, where temperatures are approximately 50 degrees Fahrenheit year-round. Water circulating through the pipe is warmed or cooled by the surrounding earth before a heat pump installed in the basement of each new home provides additional heating or cooling depending on the time of year.
Dandelion’s drilling team can complete boreholes for one or more homes per day. If they had to drill a similar installation elsewhere for a single building, they could lose an entire day simply transporting the rig to and from the site.
Installing the devices across dozens of similar new homes at once also eliminates the need for custom plans for each building and avoids potentially costly retrofits to the buildings’ heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems.
The end result is a highly efficient heating and cooling system that Dandelion says outcompetes air-source heat pumps and conventional gas heating systems. This is especially true during cold snaps, when energy demand peaks and ground-source heat pumps use a quarter as much electricity as air-source heat pumps, Yates said.
It’s “the only system that actually reduces peak demand and electrifies homes at the same time,” he said.
The Ken Caryl Ranch development is part of a larger initiative the company launched with Lennar in 2025 to install geothermal heating and cooling at more than 1,500 homes in Colorado over two years. Dandelion hopes to scale up to 10,000 homes per year nationwide in the coming years.
“Our mission at Dandelion is to mainstream geothermal, and we think that the time has finally arrived for that to happen,” Yates said.
Just over a million U.S. homes have ground-source heat pumps, with approximately 100,000 new installations each year, according to a 2025 U.S. Department of Energy report. The agency found that geothermal heating and cooling could reach 7 million homes by 2035. Doing so would reduce winter peak energy demand by more than 40 gigawatts nationwide, resulting in roughly $4 billion in annual savings in U.S. electric grid costs, according to the report.

Ground-source heat pumps currently make up just a small fraction of new home heating and cooling systems. By contrast, 3.6 million air-source heat pumps were sold in the U.S. last year, outpacing gas furnace sales for the fourth year in a row, said Yara van Ingen, an associate with BloombergNEF’s building decarbonization team.
Ground-source heat pumps are economically viable across the continental United States, according to a study published this month in the journal iScience that considered incentives, energy costs and local climate and subsurface conditions.
“It is technically possible everywhere, and there is economic potential across all states,” said Juliet Simpson, a former research engineer at the National Laboratory of the Rockies and the study’s lead author.
A primary challenge for ground-source heat pumps is their upfront cost, which averages around $25,000 for a typical new home, according to the Energy Department report. Van Ingen added that space constraints, especially in dense urban environments, as well as permitting requirements that vary across the U.S. can also complicate borehole drilling.
Dandelion and Lennar, an investor in the geothermal company, are among those working to lower costs. But incentives and policy changes also help. An energy efficiency program by Xcel Energy, Colorado’s largest gas and electric utility company, provides approximately $25,000 per home for new, high-efficiency buildings with a ground-source heat pump to offset added building and heat pump costs.
“For large neighborhoods with hundreds of homes, builders may receive seven-figure rebate amounts,” an Xcel spokesperson said in a written statement.
The rebates help Xcel advance its climate goals and meet Colorado’s Clean Heat Standard requirement to reduce greenhouse gas emissions 22 percent below 2015 levels by 2030.

A sprawling reservoir under construction south of Lake Okeechobee that Gov. Ron DeSantis has characterized as the “crown jewel” of Everglades restoration will not be enough to save Florida’s treasured and troubled river of grass, according to a new report.
The report, prepared by Friends of the Everglades, an advocacy group, suggests the Everglades needs an even larger reservoir in the Everglades Agricultural Area that at 77,000 acres and 13 feet deep would dwarf the EAA reservoir already under construction among the vast sugarcane fields in the region. That $3.5 billion reservoir, once complete, will be the largest of its kind the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has built anywhere in the country.
The report was based on an expansive review of the existing scientific literature, which taken together suggests 1 million acre-feet of water storage, in addition to the EAA reservoir, is needed in the Everglades Agricultural Area to replenish the river of grass, said Tom Van Lent, science advisor for Friends of the Everglades, who prepared the report. The water storage also would help spare fragile coastal estuaries in the region from harmful flows of polluted water from Lake Okeechobee.
“It would look like a very large but relatively shallow lake on the landscape, so it would be like a much smaller Lake Okeechobee,” Van Lent said. “I’m not oblivious to this is a difficult ask. Short-term considerations always seem to dominate longer-term investments, and that is what this would be, is a long-term investment in the viability of south Florida.”
The EAA reservoir is the centerpiece of the $27 billion effort to restore the Everglades, the watershed that spans much of the peninsula, from the headwaters of the Kissimmee River to Florida Bay at the state’s southernmost tip, and supports the drinking water supply for millions of Floridians. A series of historic attempts to drain the river of grass has made modern Florida possible and caused a litany of problems across the state’s most important freshwater resource.
In 2018, the lake’s flows to coastal estuaries contributed to a widespread outbreak of toxic algae that sickened Floridians and wiped out wildlife statewide. The calamity coincided with DeSantis’ gubernatorial campaign that year, and during his two terms in office the Republican governor has made Everglades restoration and particularly the EAA reservoir a priority.
Under his leadership, the state has invested billions of dollars toward the massive restoration effort, even as his administration has faced widespread condemnation and federal litigation over Alligator Alcatraz, the migrant detention facility that operated for a year in the Everglades before closing this summer. DeSantis announced a deal last year with the Trump administration to expedite the reservoir’s construction, with completion now scheduled for 2029.
“These historic investments have tripled water storage capacity in South Florida, accelerated critical restoration efforts, and produced measurable environmental results, including Florida Bay reaching its salinity targets for the first time in decades,” according to a statement the South Florida Water Management District, the state agency overseeing Everglades restoration, provided to Inside Climate News.
In a statement, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the federal agency overseeing the restoration effort, characterized the EAA reservoir as a key project “designed to improve the quantity, quality, timing and distribution of water moving south from Lake Okeechobee to the Everglades while helping reduce harmful discharges to the northern estuaries.”
The corps statement says that “construction milestones this year have included significant progress on the reservoir foundation and embankment, as well as completion of a major controlled construction operation at the reservoir site. The accelerated project is a clear example of Building Infrastructure, Not Paperwork in action.”
Historically, the Everglades’ freshwater coursed lazily and shallow among the sawgrass south of Lake Okeechobee, between the banks of the Atlantic Coastal Ridge to the east and highlands of what now are part of the Big Cypress National Preserve to the west. Recapturing as much of this water as possible is at the heart of the restoration effort.
The Friends of the Everglades’ report said locating more water storage in the Everglades Agricultural Area would replicate the natural flow of the river of grass, while north of Lake Okeechobee the water storage would benefit primarily the lake and coastal estuaries but not the Everglades. The mind-boggling size of the additional reservoir proposed in the report was based on an analysis of land and levee costs and ecological function. By comparison the EAA reservoir, at 10,000 acres and 24 feet deep, is designed to hold 240,000 acre-feet of water, a quarter of what the report recommended.
The findings were similar to those of a 2015 University of Florida Water Institute report authorized by the Florida Senate to identify alternatives to the damaging lake flows to the coastal estuaries. That report called for 1 million acre-feet of water storage north and south of the lake, along with 400,000 acre-feet to the west and 200,000 acre-feet to the east.
The report was produced before the EAA reservoir was conceptualized, additional reservoirs were constructed on either side of the lake and a new management plan was implemented for Lake Okeechobee. “The path forward requires significant long-term investment in the infrastructure of the South Florida hydrologic system,” the report said.
Van Lent and other environmental groups had raised concerns about the EAA reservoir’s design before construction began in 2023. The groups voiced reservations about whether the reservoir would convey enough water south or clean the water to established standards. The groups also said the design failed to factor in climate change, among other issues.

When Nicole Williams moved into her house in Pennsylvania’s North Centre Township in 2011, it was a homecoming. She’d spent the first few years of her life a half-mile down the road in Brookside Village, a tidy community of 170 mobile homes nestled between the west branch of Briar Creek and a farm that grew sweet corn and pumpkins just up the hill. Her new colonial revival with expansive views of the Susquehanna Valley’s rolling landscape was one of several houses built on land that once belonged to that farm.
Fifteen years later, Williams has three kids between 11 and 16, two English bulldogs and an in-line water filtration system in her basement whose two sturdy tanks remove the toxic chemicals leaching from the neighboring farm into her well.
The chemicals in Williams’ well are among a class of thousands known collectively as per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS, colloquially called “forever chemicals” because they don’t break down naturally. They were present in the sewage sludge the nearby farm received from the local water treatment plant and spread on its fields as fertilizer beginning sometime in the 1980s. For two years, the state Department of Environmental Protection has been investigating the groundwater plume emanating from the farm and around a dozen other sites in Columbia County that also utilized the sludge.
The investigation is the state’s first in the region, but the crisis in North Centre “is the tip of the iceberg,” said Lane Whigham, director of the Alliance for Aquatic Resource Monitoring—which goes by ALLARM—at Dickinson College in Carlisle. His group’s volunteers test water quality throughout the Chesapeake Bay watershed, including Columbia County. The Department of Environmental Protection found elevated levels of PFAS in Briar Creek and has cautioned residents not to eat fish caught there. That warning is likely just the beginning of what’s needed, according to Whigham.
A 2023 study led by the U.S. Geological Survey found that 76 percent of Pennsylvania streams contained at least one PFAS. In 2025, the Three Rivers Waterkeeper tested 39 sites in Western Pennsylvania and found PFAS in 74 percent. When it comes to these chemicals in the state’s waterways, “it’s not a matter of ‘if’ anymore, it’s ‘how much,’” Whigham said.
Consuming high levels of PFAS—used in a wide range of industrial processes and consumer products—can pose a risk to reproductive and developmental health, hinder the body’s immune system and hormones and contribute to a variety of cancers, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.
In 2024, the agency established drinking water standards for six PFAS chemicals, including limits of 4 parts per trillion (ppt) for PFOA and PFOS, two of the most prominent. That fall, the Williams’ water tested at 182.4 total ppt. PFOA in their water was eight times the EPA limit; PFOS was 32 times the limit.
Among 80 residential wells tested by state environmental regulators during their investigation, 23 had rates above the Williams’, reaching as high as 3,612 total ppt.
The worrying presence of PFAS in sewage sludge—the semi-solid, nutrient-rich material left after wastewater treatment, referred to by the waste industry as biosolids—was first identified in Maine in 2016. Well testing revealed elevated levels on a dairy farm there. The farm’s milk was also contaminated, and further testing has identified tainted water on more than 100 farms and 500 residential properties in the state.
Maine became the first state to ban the use of sludge on farmland in 2022. Pennsylvania, like nearly every other state, still allows the practice. Its use as fertilizer has long been encouraged by both federal and state agencies.
The Department of Environmental Protection estimates that 400,000 tons of sludge are applied to land in Pennsylvania annually. More than 40 percent of that total ends up on farmland, according to the National Biosolids Data Project, a group whose partners include industry members and municipal entities. Since 1997, more than 1,100 Pennsylvania farms have been permitted to apply sludge, and 740 of those permits are still active.
“If your boat is filling up with water, you need to plug the hole first,” said Stephanie Wein, a water and conservation advocate at the nonprofit PennEnvironment. “They’re just letting this stuff continue to be applied.”
The investigation in North Centre has alerted residents to the hazards in their community and stopped the consumption of tainted water. Across Pennsylvania, though, the extent of the risk posed by PFAS-contaminated sludge is unknown. A full accounting would require a testing program that could tally the toll of decades of sludge application on rural communities reliant on private wells. More than a quarter of Pennsylvania residents get their water from a private well.
An adequate response is complicated by the fact that forever chemicals are colorless, odorless and tasteless—not to mention highly persistent—and therefore undetectable without the right test.
Williams, a pediatric registered nurse, had her well water tested when she moved in, but PFAS isn’t among the pollutants typically tested, so it wasn’t caught. Now, she’s left to wonder how her children’s health might be affected by a childhood spent drinking polluted water. And she can’t help but question what’s lurking in the groundwater in rural communities across the state.
“You drive through the countryside and you no longer see these beautiful fields,” Williams said. “You look at fields and you’re like, ‘I wonder if these fields are contaminated or if these houses are OK.’”
Discovering a PFAS Crisis
The first indication that something was wrong in Columbia County came from Brookside Village, Williams’ first home.

From our collaborating partner Living on Earth, public radio’s environmental news magazine, an interview by Paloma Beltran with Tanuja Pandey, a climate justice activist in Nepal.
In the weeks following the deadly glacier collapse and floods in Nepal this August, researchers from the World Weather Attribution group rapidly assessed the event and concluded that climate change played a “very strong” role in the catastrophe.
Warmer weather melted ice, thawed permafrost and increased rainfall, destabilizing a glacier before its collapse. Nepal estimates that damages from the floods—which killed at least 1,300 people—could exceed $4 billion, over a tenth of the country’s total gross domestic product.
Tanuja Pandey is a climate justice activist and lawyer based in Kathmandu, Nepal. She originally hails from Sudur Paschim, a region affected by the floods, and is co-founder and chair of Harin Nepal, an intersectional climate justice organization. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
PALOMA BELTRAN: It’s been nearly a month since devastating floods hit Nepal and Tibet due to glacial collapse in the Himalayas. What have you seen in the weeks since the disaster? How are you and your community holding up?
TANUJA PANDEY: Life after a flood is incredibly difficult, especially for those who have lost someone they love. The water may eventually recede, but the grief does not. Imagine waking up every morning knowing that the person you share your room, your home, your meals, your life with is no longer there. Some of the families are still waiting for their loved ones to be found, while others are trying to give a final farewell without having the chance to properly say goodbye. Then they are expected to rebuild their home, return to their work and somehow continue with their lives.
We often see the images of flood when the water is rising, but we don’t see enough of what happens afterward. It’s quite traumatizing to see everything. When we talk about floods, we talk about the water, the death toll, the missing persons. But for communities, the real story continues long after the water disappears. They are left rebuilding the homes and livelihoods, memories, dignity and sometimes their entire sense of security. That is what Nepal is going through right now, and it’s really traumatizing to see everything and to feel helpless because all we can give is sympathy at the moment, even though we want to help with everything.
BELTRAN: You visited the affected zones in Nepal. What did you see?
PANDEY: I saw the life fading away. I saw the children waiting for their parents. I saw the wife waiting for her husband, a mother waiting for their child and I saw the entire community swept away. It used to be one of the Indigenous lands of Nepal, and the community—who did nothing to contribute to climate change—lost everything within seconds.
Nepal is a very religious country. They worship nature. Even today, a lot of climatic disaster is related not to the anthropologic reason, but to the demonic factor. People don’t know what climate change actually is, and I saw people not praying this time. It was quite heavy for us to see everything, and even heavy for us to talk about it now.
BELTRAN: Nepal estimates that the recovery from the disaster will cost more than $4 billion. What are the non-economic costs that the world should consider regarding this catastrophe?
PANDEY: Economic cost is important, but we don’t talk about the amount of anxiety the community has gone through, the amount of fear we have. A lot of people in mountain communities who live downstream are migrating after the event because people are scared to live near the water resources. Nepal’s traditional settlements have always been near the riverside. It’s quite hard to talk about it because we are giving up on our identity, our traditional way of living, just because few countries refuse to stick to their commitment.
BELTRAN: In the days following the flood, Nepal’s government wrote to the United Nations Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage; Nepal is requesting $20 million. That’s the maximum amount a country can request, and Nepal framed the request in terms of climate justice rather than a request for aid. Tell us about that distinction.
PANDEY: The problem is that Nepal’s climate story often becomes internationally visible only after a disaster reaches a catastrophic death toll. But in fact, we lose our people—amounting to hundreds— every year. It has become a new normal to us, and that creates a dangerous cycle. The world responds to the headline event rather than to [the] underlying accumulating loss and damage.
“We are giving up on our identity, our traditional way of living, just because few countries refuse to stick to their commitment.”
Nepal has done its part. We have restored our forests on an impressive scale, and we are rapidly moving toward clean energy, even though people don’t know what clean energy actually is. We are promoting electric mobility and implementing the climate adaptation plan at the local level. We are even going back to our traditional knowledge, Indigenous practices.
A country responsible for less than 0.02 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions is paying an even higher price for a crisis it did not create. … We are not here to blame any nation, but demand what is rightfully ours. We demand solidarity and to seek the solution because at this moment, we want international communities and polluting countries to stick to it.
BELTRAN: From what I understand, Nepal has still not received any money from the U.N. fund. This pot of money is severely underfunded because wealthy nations have not contributed what they initially pledged. For example, the United States withdrew from the fund in 2025. What role do wealthier nations have to play in addressing this crisis?

Brazilian President Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva has announced a ban on online gambling, just days before an election in which he is seeking a fourth term as the country's leader.
Lula, who is running against the son of the incarcerated former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, signed a provisional order on Friday that "prohibits all sports betting and online casinos".
The online gambling industry in Brazil was legalised in 2018 and has since been blamed for widespread household income losses due to addiction.
Lula described the industry as a "cancer" in his announcement, adding "either we remove the tumour, or it kills us".
The move comes just over a week before the first round of voting in Brazil's presidential election. Recent polls have the 80-year-old leader almost neck-and-neck with FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro.
The new measures must receive congressional approval within 120 days to remain in force.
Lula acknowledged online betting was created under the former President Michel Temer's administration but that it "grew without regulation under Bolsonaro's management", in a statement on X .
He said that there were "no restrictions" particularly for preventing children and adolescents from accessing online betting.
"We won't allow betting companies to profit at the expense of Brazilian families' income and lives," the president added.
The president described how he had heard from families who had sold everything in their houses because of their gambling addictions.
Separate to the online betting order, Lula also signed a bill to penalise criminal offences related to fixed-odds betting.
Earlier this week, at the United Nations General Assembly, Lula accused the industry of "transforming addiction into profit".
But FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro called the gambling crackdown "populist, hypocritical and politically motivated" during a campaign rally in Rio de Janeiro on Friday, according to Reuters.
Most types of gambling, such as casinos and slot machines, are illegal in Brazil, but ever since online betting was legalised in 2018, it has exploded in popularity.
About 59.9% of Brazilian adults support banning internet betting, a survey by Atlas and Bloomberg published this week has found.

At least two people have died and four more are missing after an explosion destroyed a building housing a holiday rental property in the historic centre of Athens.
The blast happened in the Plaka area of the Greek capital, a neighbourhood close to tourist sites such as the Acropolis, with local media reporting the building housed a holiday rental.
An American man and woman have died, with two more US tourists missing, AFP news agency reported citing local officials. A Greek national and UK national who lived in the building are also said to be missing.
Pictures from the scene showed emergency service workers searching through rubble, with a gas leak the suspected cause of the blast.
The body of a woman was found on Saturday morning, with a Greek fire official later telling reporters the body of a man had also been found.
The tourists were confirmed to be missing when they did not arrive for their flight at Athens airport, Reuters news agency reported citing local police.
Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said: "We are talking about an incredible disaster."
The three-storey building completely collapsed due to the force of the blast, with neighbouring buildings damaged and debris scattered across the road.
Local media reported people were injured by material scattered across nearby streets and some buildings needed to be evacuated.
Excavators and thermal imaging cameras have been used at the scene to search for survivors.
The explosion happened on a small road situated between two of Athens' most visited sites - the Acropolis and the Temple of Olympian Zeus.
BBC News has contacted the UK Foreign Office.

A project to preserve vulnerable vegetation and wildlife will see hundreds of wildflower plants introduced to an upland hay meadow.
Friends of the Lake District (Fold) wants to plant 1,500 wildflowers on land at Mazonwath, in Little Asby, Cumbria, to help reintroduce many native species lost through some farming practices.
A spokesperson for the environmental charity said plant roots were good for moisture retention and soil health, with their texture playing a part in slowing the flow of overland water.
They added: "Conservation work like this is really important to help our insects and birds have a home into the future."
Fold is calling for volunteers to help join the planting efforts on 13 October and more information on how to join is available on the charity's website.
The charity will be planting great burnet, bird's foot trefoil, black knapweed, cranesbills, oxeye daisy and vetches.
The organisation is working with Cumbria Wildlife Trust as part of the Cumbria Seed Bank Project, which aims to reverse the decline of grassland habitats in the county.
The two-year project in partnership with Kew Millennium Seed Bank, aims to collect, store and sow seed from rare and declining grassland species that are found in Cumbria.
A Fold spokesperson said: "The aim is not only to introduce harder-to-establish plants that are missing from grasslands, but to also use this project to inform future work to safeguard vulnerable populations of plant species in Cumbria, so that these wildflower species are not lost forever."

693e10278b81.text: The U.S. and China have agreed to set up a dialogue on artificial intelligence , with a communications channel to help defuse serious incidents, the White House said overnight. Why it matters: President Trump has said the main thing that matters in the AI race is beating China — but the pact acknowledges that they're serious competition, too. Driving the news: The White House released a fact sheet late Friday night with outcomes from Trump's summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. The two sides agreed to refer to AI as "super intelligence" or "SI," the White House said — Trump's new and preferred term for the technology. They will create a "U.S.-China Super Intelligence (SI) Dialogue" to meet on "risks and benefits related to SI," with the next meeting by November. Zoom in: The administration also said there would be a "bilateral communication channel for SI incidents," which some have likened to a Cold War-era " red telephone " between the two nations. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent focused on creating the channel during last weekend's pre-summit meetings with Chinese officials. Yes, but: It's not clear what kind of incidents would rise to the level of using the channel, or what kinds of notifications each side would give the other.

Butterfly and day-flying moth numbers recorded across Devon and Cornwall this summer have been "very good" - but experts fear prolonged hot and dry weather could lead to a decline.
Nearly 5,000 people took part in the Butterfly Conservation's 2026 big butterfly count in Devon, recording 77,151 insects during the three-week count. It said nearly 3,000 people took part in Cornwall, spotting 47,712.
Head of science at the conservation, professor Richard Fox, said adult butterflies loved hot weather, but warned we could be on course "for a population crash".
"The extreme droughts in 1976 and 1995 had severe impacts on butterfly populations, with some species never fully recovering," he said.
The charity said strong butterfly numbers was "likely" down to favourable conditions for caterpillars in spring, followed by the hot, sunny weather enjoyed by adult butterflies during the summer months.
However, it said previous drought conditions across much of the UK may have caused food plants used by caterpillars to wither before they had finished feeding. The charity fears the full impact may not become clear until next year.
Fox said many species were already under pressure, with 80% of the UK's butterfly populations having declined since the 1970s.
"So many are already struggling for survival, without these extreme weather pressures," Fox said.
'Pushed towards extinction'
He added: "With increasingly hot, dry summers and droughts predicted to become more and more frequent due to climate breakdown, degraded habitats and already depleted butterfly populations, some species may be pushed further and faster towards extinction, which is a very sombre thought.
"They are, quite simply, less resilient to these events, which means we could be looking at very difficult years ahead."
The charity is urging people to help wildlife recover by planting more trees and shrubs, installing water butts to store rainwater and leaving areas of grass uncut.
Most spotted butterfly species
The Gatekeeper was the most commonly spotted butterfly in Devon and Cornwall.
The Meadow Brown took the second spot in Devon, followed by the Red Admiral. In Cornwall, the Red Admiral took second spot, followed by the Painted Lady.
Butterfly Conservation said the Painted Lady was one of the standout species with 6,955 recorded in Devon and 6,033 in Cornwall. The migratory butterfly enjoyed a strong year nationally.
Painted Ladies undertake one of the world's most remarkable insect migrations, travelling from Africa to the UK over several generations, crossing the Sahara Desert and Mediterranean Sea.

4ae45be2a017.text: The U.S. and China have reached a deal to lower tariffs on $30 billion of "non-sensitive goods" as part of a trade package agreed at this week's summit between President Trump and Xi Jinping, the White House said. Why it matters: Such a deal would mark a thaw in the trade war that engulfed the two countries last year. As laid out by the White House, it would also potentially lower prices on a variety of consumer goods where American shoppers have felt the pinch of inflation. How it works: The Trump administration said China would lower its tariffs on some agricultural goods and seafood, wood products, cosmetics, and medical devices. The U.S. will cut tariffs on small appliances, toys, holiday decorations, and kids' car seats. Between the lines: The White House also said China would import 10 million metric tons of U.S. coal in 2027 and again in 2028. The country was a top-five importer of U.S. coal until slashing imports in 2025 amid the trade war. The intrigue: The fact sheet released by the White House was more vague on the fate of the crucial rare earth minerals that have been at the heart of the trade dispute. "The United States and China continue to work on U.S. concerns regarding supply chain shortages related to rare earths and other critical minerals, with the goal of ensuring shipment levels return to appropriate levels," it said,.

The Republic of Ireland have delayed the pre-match news conference planned for Sunday's Uefa Nations League game against Israel in Hungary - a fixture campaigners have called on them to boycott.
Heimir Hallgrimsson's team are scheduled to meet Israel in Debrecen at 19:45 BST, with the return fixture in Backa Topola, Serbia on 4 October.
They have faced calls to withdraw from the games because of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war with a "Stop The Game" campaign - organised by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine - gathering pace.
Former Republic of Ireland manager Brian Kerr and ex-international James McClean are among those to have backed calls for a boycott.
However, there are also Irish supporters, perhaps less vocal, who have always believed that the match should be played with supporters in attendance.
Following Thursday's 1-0 defeat by Kosovo, midfielder Jason Knight opined he didn't think "the game should be going ahead", while winger Chiedozie Ogbene urged the public to not "put the pressure on us" regarding their approach to the scheduled game.
Hallgrimsson and a player were scheduled to meet the media at 09:15 BST (10.15 local time), before training, but the conference was delayed shortly beforehand.
A Uefa official entered the room to inform waiting media teams that the press conference was postponed until after training, which would have been about 11:30 BST (12.30 local time).
But shortly afterwards, the Uefa official returned to the media room to announce that the Republic of Ireland's training session had also been postponed, with no time given for when it might take place. There is also no confirmed time for the news conference.
The fixture has been embroiled in controversy since the two teams were drawn to play each other in Group B3.
A team meeting took place on Friday for players to air their views on Sunday's game and the return fixture in Serbia.
The players were expected to release a statement at Saturday's news conference, but the delay has added further uncertainty, with some reports of at least one player wishing to withdraw from the squad.
It has since emerged the news conference, scheduled to take place at the stadium, is now set to be staged at the team hotel, with Uefa unable to provide information regarding the delay.
The armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.
In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

Hundreds of thousands of people have greeted Pope Leo XIV in the centre of Paris for a giant open-air Mass.
Crowds cheered as the pontiff moved down the Champs-ÃlysÃ©es Avenue beneath the Arc de Triomphe, waving to crowds from his popemobile.
The head of the Catholic Church blessed several babies as he stopped at different stages along the avenue as chants of "Leo, Leo" rang out.
More than half a million people are expected to attend the event in the heart of the French capital on Saturday and a special altar has been built on the Place de la Concorde for the ceremony.
French President Emmanuel Macron, who met Leo for an hour of talks on Friday, will not be at any of the Pope's Masses during his four-day visit to France, largely to avoid breaching France's strict separation of state and religion.
But the Champs-ÃlysÃ©es Mass will be attended by Macron's wife Brigitte and Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu.
Several candidates for next year's presidential election are also expected to attend.
Marine Le Pen of the hard-right National Rally party and conservative Bruno Retailleau were both pictured at the Place de la Concorde ahead of the event, while centrists Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal are also due to be there.
Mayor of Le Havre and former French Prime Minister Edouard Philippe and former Prime Minister Francois Fillon were both also seen at the Place de la Concorde.
Earlier on Saturday, the Pope met migrants as he visited the Maison Bakhita centre, an association supporting refugees, and praised the organisation for inviting "us to see those who are invisible".
During the visit Leo said it was "possible to encounter one another and to live together in dignity and peace".
He also stressed the "the fundamental role of women in building a civilisation of love".
The Pope also issued a warning about the dangers of artificial intelligence (AI) at the start of his visit to France on Friday.
Leo cautioned against "losing our humanity amid a paradise of machines" in wide-ranging remarks to Church and state officials at the ÃlysÃ©e Palace.
Large crowds are expected throughout the pontiff's trip, which the Church believes reflects a growing spirituality among the French and other Europeans.
On Sunday, 150,000 have signed up to attend mass in the Pyrenean sanctuary of Lourdes.
The Pope will be in Metz, in northeast France, on Monday where he will pay tribute to Robert Schuman (1886-1963), a founding father of the European Union and a fervent Catholic who is today a candidate for beatification.
Born in Chicago in 1955, Pope Leo XIV was originally called Robert Prevost â a French name.
His paternal grandmother was born in Le Havre in Normandy in 1894. When she married in the US many years later, she and her Italian husband took the name Prevost, which had been her mother's maiden name.

831f6c59c7b7.text: President Trump told voters to pretend he's on the ballot. Apparently they're listening: Republicans coast to coast are getting pulled under by a violent undertow fueled by Trump's unpopularity. Why it matters: It's looked bad for Republicans all year, but this week felt different — like the political environment was disintegrating in real time, one ominous data point after another. Most worrisome for the GOP, there's virtually no chance the war ends, inflation cools, interest rates fall, consumer confidence rises, and economic optimism surges before the Nov. 3 election. That's why Republicans fear the undertow imperils so many candidates once deemed safe. The big picture: Predicting election outcomes is a risky business, but it may be time to expand the imagination of how ugly it could get for Republicans five weeks from now. Start with mood music: This week, Trump's disapproval rating hit 60.4%, the worst mark of his two terms in office, including the aftermath of the Jan. 6 riots. Gas prices are over $4 a gallon, diesel has hit $6.50 and no relief is in sight. Seven months in, the U.S. is locked in a standoff with Iran with no apparent exit strategy. Grocery prices are still rising year over year. Mortgage rates hit 7%. And the cost of borrowing across the economy continues to climb. Enter the elections: The problems for the GOP are everywhere. In the battle for the Senate, once ruby-red Texas looks more in play than ever, and Florida isn't far behind. Nor is Alaska. North Carolina and Georgia look lost. Maine is problematic. The Senate GOP campaign arm is begging donors for another $8.9 million to defend Senate seats in three states that Trump won by double digits two years ago — Alaska, Iowa and Ohio. "We're having problems just getting Republican voters to respond to polls," said one national Republican pollster. "At what point do we think these guys aren't showing up at the actual polls on Election Day?" Only in Michigan do Republicans see glimmers of hope to pick up a Senate seat because Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed is seen by some as so radical that he has "scared the shit out of our people to want to vote," the GOP pollster said. "But even then, in this environment, who knows?" What once looked like a long shot for Democrats — taking control of the Senate by flipping four Republican-held seats on a map favoring the GOP — looks increasingly plausible. On the House side, the Cook Political Report moved 15 House races toward Democrats on Friday. Democrats need to net just three seats to win control of the chamber. Republicans are now playing defense deep in red America. GOP-aligned groups are spending money in more than a half-dozen districts that Trump won by at least 15 points in 2024. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) is keeping expectations low on what a good Election Night will look like. He told Axios that Republicans might be able to get 225 House seats. It takes 218 to have a majority. What they're saying: "While many have long predicted that Democrats will enjoy a 'blue wave' election, I think of it more as a 'red undertow,' which will pull many Republicans under and significantly trim the margins for many others, said the Cook Report's founder and top elections handicapper Charlie Cook. That's an implied reminder that Democrats' favorability ratings aren't good; they're just better than Republicans'. "Over the last 90 days," Cook added, "President Trump's political standing has transitioned from very unpopular to toxic and now to radioactive." Said another consultant involved with races across the country: "Things were bad. But they started to go worse recently and if it keeps on this track, it's gonna be real bad." The environment is starting to rival the second midterm election of President George W. Bush's tenure in 2006, the consultant said, amid the Iraq war and the botched response to Hurricane Katrina. Republicans lost control of both chambers after losing 30 House seats and six Senate seats. "The numbers are somewhere between shitabulous and craptastic," a top Republican advising several federal races across the country told Axios. "It looks worse than 2018 now. Trump is heading to Bush 2006 levels." State of play: More and more lately, Republican incumbents are running for cover from Trump. In Iowa, two House Republicans have switched their positions to support a war powers resolution on Iran. Sen. Chuck Grassley, who rode the 1980 Republican wave to the Senate, and Rep. Ashley Hinson, who's running for Iowa's other Senate seat, are demanding restrictions on diesel exports. The other side: One Trump adviser downplayed the GOP tremors, pointing to the Republicans' massive cash advantage. "If we execute and our people show up, it's a different ballgame," the adviser said. "There's more than a month to go." "Look, things aren't peachy," the adviser acknowledged. "But it's a presidential midterm. Things are hairy. Things always get hairy for any White House at this time."

(AP) — More than 70,000 customers were without electricity in the U.S. Northeast on Saturday, the effect of a powerful nor'easter expected to create dangerous conditions through the weekend. Forecasters warned of gale winds that could down trees and heavy rain that could put roads underwater. Tens of millions of people are in the path of the storm was already beginning to lash the region with strong winds and rain as the region braces for much more. Dangerous flooding is expected along the Mid-Atlantic coast, particularly near New Jersey and Delaware, according to the National Weather Service. "This storm is expected to bring major coastal flooding to the Mid-Atlantic Coast over multiple high tide cycles through the weekend," the weather service said Saturday. "Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses." READ MORE: Nor'easter to lash the East Coast with strong winds, flooding and heavy rain In the coastal New Jersey borough of Surf City, water, with waves rippling along its surface, flooded the streets, inundating some homes. About 34 miles (54.7 kilometers) up the coast in the borough of Manasquan, where some roads were also flooding, Mayor Mike Mangan said he expected "a lot of water in the streets for a long time." A voluntary evacuation had been issued earlier in some low-lying areas of the community. Concerts were canceled, along with dozens of flights going into airports in Boston, Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard on Friday and Saturday. Several airlines were offering to waive some change or cancellation fees for some East Coast flights through the weekend. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul urged people to use caution. She said coastal flooding is the biggest threat, but it will also bring heavy rains, powerful winds and waves as high as 20 feet (six meters). "The rain is underway and while it's only half an inch or so thus far, mark my words: Much more is coming," the governor said. New Jersey communities prepare for major flooding Matty Guarino pulls Crew Guarino on a paddleboard in a flooded area after heavy rain from a nor'easter fell as a strong coastal storm batters the U.S. northeast coast, in Surf City, New Jersey, on Sept. 26, 2026. Photo by Vincent Alban/Reuters Brian Kelly, the mayor of the tiny New Jersey beach community Sea Bright, said the borough is bracing for winds up to 50 mph (80 kph) and flooding that could reach up to 6 feet (1.8 meters) on some streets. Officials expect the flooding to start Saturday and worsen by midday. "It's going to be worse than average. We do have probably one or two flooding events a year, sometimes more, sometimes less, but I think this one will be closer to an Irene-scale flooding event," Kelly said, referencing the 2011 storm that caused major flooding in the Northeast. "I hope I'm wrong, but that's my gut feeling." Kelly hopes hundreds of residents living in low-lying areas will consider evacuating. He said the town will open its recreation center for evacuees. Damaging winds threaten coastal New England Peak wind gusts could approach 60 to 65 mph (97 to 105 kph) on Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket on Friday night and Saturday, compared with about 50 to 55 mph (80 to 89 kph) around Boston and 35 to 40 mph (56 to 64 kph) farther inland, according to Matthew Belk, a meteorologist with NWS in Norton, Massachusetts. "It's definitely going to be a case of the closer to the coast you are, the more impacts from the storm you're likely to see," Belk said. LIVE MAP: Track the path of Hurricane Polo Belk said nor'easters are not unusual as New England moves into fall, but one concern this early in the season is that leaves remain on the trees, creating more wind resistance. That could increase the risk of downed limbs, which in turn can cause power outages and leave debris in roads, he said. Along the Atlantic coasts of New Jersey and Delaware, wind gusts could reach 60 mph (96.6 kph), according to NWS. In southeastern Connecticut and eastern Long Island, New York, gusts could get almost as high, potentially downing tree limbs and power lines. Storm disrupts concerts, baseball and flights Air travel was also being disrupted, with Boston particularly hard hit. Flight-tracking service FlightAware reported 39 cancellations at Boston Logan International Airport between 6 a.m. and 10 a.m. Saturday, compared with 22 at New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport. Another 12 flights were delayed at Logan. Meanwhile, the Red Sox announced their weekend series against the Chicago Cubs would be adjusted. The team moved the Sunday afternoon game to Friday to create a split doubleheader. Separately, Ed Sheeran announced that his high-profile Friday and Saturday shows at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, would be canceled due to the storm. The public ferry service connecting Cape Cod with the islands of Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard was experiencing widespread cancellations Friday due to strong winds and choppy water. In Rhode Island, ferries were also canceled for Block Island. The disrupted ferry service was expected to also spill into Saturday. An independent review has pointed to a number of security shortcomings at the Utah campus where conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot dead last year.
The report said Utah Valley University (UVU) did not carry out a proper written security assessment nor prepare an event action plan, deferring key decision-making about the event to Kirk's conservative organisation Turning Point USA.
It also said that Kirk's aides had insisted on a outdoor venue, overriding security concerns from campus officials, who then failed to properly assess the dangers.
The 31-year-old activist had been addressing thousands of people in an Orem campus courtyard when he was shot from a nearby rooftop on 10 September 2025.
Kirk's family said the report reinforced their concerns about how the event was managed.
University officials had raised concerns in August 2025 about holding the event at a location surrounded by tall buildings and had suggested alternative venues, including some indoors, the report, external - published by UVU - says.
"But a Turning Point representative insisted that Kirk speak at a campus courtyard because he had been there previously and the organisation was familiar with the location," it adds.
Despite the "significant protective operations considerations", no line-of-sight assessment was documented in the planning process, the external consultants note.
They also identified shortcomings in the co-ordination between university police and Kirk's private security team.
A proposed meeting between the university's police chief and Turning Point security shortly before the event did not take place, the report said.
The reviewers described the absence of a joint security briefing and walk-through as a missed opportunity to have identified risks, clarified responsibilities and considered additional security measures.
However, the review concluded that no university employee or representative had acted in bad faith or shown "willful and wanton disregard" for anyone's safety.
Kirk's family has previously accused the university of serious security failures and has filed a wrongful-death notice, a step that can precede legal action.
The family's lawyer, Brett Parkinson, said the independent report released on Friday backed up the concerns raised by Kirk's loved ones.
"The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement," Parkinson said in a statement to the Associated Press. "Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU's fatal shortcomings that day."
When asked for comment on the findings, Turning Point USA referred to Parkinson's statement.
The review makes numerous recommendations aimed at improving security for major campus events.
UVU President Jon Anderson said the university must "learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations".
It has previously been reported that the campus police failed to conduct security procedures now common practice at high-profile events, including flying a drone to monitor rooftops or security screening like bag checks and metal detectors.
Kirk had been debating UVU students about US mass shootings, as part of a series of events across different university campuses, when he was shot in the neck shortly after noon. He was rushed to hospital but later pronounced dead.
His alleged killer, Tyler Robinson, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder in connection with Kirk's death. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty.

0008976498c5.text: President Trump said on Saturday that he rejected the latest Iranian proposal that was conveyed to the U.S. during indirect negotiations in New York this week. Why it matters: While Qatar and other regional mediators are trying to revive negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, the gaps on the key issues are still very wide. While Iran wants to focus any talks on the Strait of Hormuz and the U.S. naval blockade, the Trump administration demands the Iranians agree to nuclear concessions. What he is saying: "They have made a proposal and I rejected it," Trump said. But a U.S. official claimed "positive and constructive" discussions are still ongoing between the U.S. and Iran through the mediators, including on nuclear issues. Driving the news: U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held a new round of indirect negotiations with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this week. Qatari officials participated in the negotiations, passing messages between the two parties, sources with direct knowledge said. Araghchi gave Witkoff and Kushner Iran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and resuming nuclear talks. Iran proposed reopening the strait and resuming nuclear talks in a week, if the U.S. lifts its naval blockade, removes sanctions on oil sales and reinstates a ceasefire across the region. The U.S. negotiators made it clear to the Iranians during the talks on Tuesday that Iran doesn't control the strait and therefore can't make demands about it, a source told Axios. State of play: Dozens of oil tankers are transiting the strait each day under U.S. protection, moving millions of barrels of oil to global markets — still well below pre-war volumes but enough to ease some pressure. U.S. officials claim that over the last 72 hours around 60 million barrels of oil transited through the Strait of Hormuz.

But on Saturday, Trump rejected the proposal saying Iran wanted to make a deal because it was "losing so badly." Iran effectively closed the strait after the U.S. and Israel attacked the Islamic Republic in late February, and the number of ships passing through has dropped significantly because of Iranian threats and attacks on vessels in the waterway. Iranian outlets say the country's president has left New York Semiofficial media outlets in Iran reported that President Masoud Pezeshkian has left New York for Tehran after the annual U.N. gathering of world leaders. Iran's president says supreme leader, still unseen in public, has no health issues Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told CBS that, from his viewpoint as a physician, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has "no specific ongoing health issues" despite not being seen or heard in public since the war with the U.S. and Israel began in February. "But, of course, he was healthy enough to be able to withstand those hours of that situation. From a medical standpoint, he's completely healthy," the president said. When asked whether the supreme leader's face and legs have recovered, Pezeshkian responded, "Yes." Khamenei's father and other family members were killed on the opening day of the war. Saudi Arabia says it intercepted a missile fired by Houthis Saudi Arabia's military spokesperson, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, claimed early Saturday that a ballistic missile launched by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen was intercepted and destroyed. He said it was fired toward the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait. The Associated Press couldn't immediately verify that independently. There was no immediate statement of responsibility, though it can take days for the Houthis to issue one. A regional body representing Arab Gulf states, the Gulf Cooperation Council, condemned the latest Houthi attacks as a "grave escalation and threat to regional security" and urged the international community to respond. Iraq seeks exemptions to US sanctions on Iranian airlines Iraq said it is in direct contact with the U.S. to secure exemptions from sanctions on Iranian airlines as Washington continues economic pressure on Tehran. WATCH: Senate rejects war powers resolution to halt military action in Iran as gas prices upend midterms The Iraqi prime minister's office said the aim is to get exemptions for certain airports, noting flights for humanitarian reasons such as medical treatment, education and religious pilgrimages. Many pilgrims in neighboring Iran visit sites such as Karbala and Najaf. Trump again posts a map calling key waterway 'Trump Strait' Before rejecting Iran's proposal Saturday, Trump posted an image on his Truth Social platform of the Strait of Hormuz labeled "Trump Strait." It is not the first time he has tried to antagonize Iran in this way. The White House on Friday said only that U.S. officials were having positive and constructive conversations with mediators on the Iran war. Earlier in the week, Iran and the U.S. participated in hours of indirect talks. - Published
There has been a wave of criticism in Germany after the town of Heidenau, near Dresden in Saxony, decided to ban "stumbling stone" memorials to victims of the Nazis.
Germany's Education Minister Karin Prien told newspaper Bild that the ban was a "scandal".
Since the 1990s, many towns in countries across Europe, including in Germany and Austria, have embedded small brass plaques in the streets in memory of Jews and other victims of Nazi atrocities.
The plaques, called Stolpersteine in German, are often placed outside the houses where the victims used to live or work. They are frequently funded by donations.
But now councillors from the Alternative fÃ¼r Deutschland (AfD) party and the conservative CDU in Heidenau have voted to ban stumbling stones - or "Stolpersteine" in German - in their town.
The AfD in Saxony has been classified as extreme-right by German intelligence, a designation the party rejects.
The motion in the town council said that many citizens felt that this form of commemoration of Nazi victims was inappropriate.
Memorials should in future be placed at the city's Nordfriedhof cemetery to make it "impossible to step directly onto the memorial elements", the motion stated.
However, Karin Prien, a member of the CDU, criticised the decision.
"Anyone who banishes Stolpersteine and memorial sites commemorating Jewish life from public spaces to the cemetery is prioritising death over life and rendering Jewish people invisible once again," she told Bild.
She said her own CDU party in Saxony also bore responsibility for the decision.
Charlotte Knobloch, a Holocaust survivor and president of the Jewish Community in Munich, said that removing memorials from the cityscape was "completely the wrong approach".
She told the Funke Media Group that she was "appalled that a democratic party would stoop to supporting such a transparent manoeuvre by the extremists of the AfD".
Knobloch said that she was not a supporter of the stumbling stones, but added that "decentralised remembrance â which is not banished from public space but, on the contrary, permeates and shapes it" was crucial to a genuine culture of remembrance.
In her own city of Munich, there are no Stolpersteine on municipal land. Instead, the city allows memorial plaques on public buildings.
As the name suggests, Stolpersteine are intended as memorials people stumble upon, making them reflect on the history of their location.
Gunter Demnig, the artist who initiated the Stolperstein project, said that given the recent electoral successes of the AfD "it was certainly to be expected that something like this would happen".
The AfD recently secured major victories in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.
Some branches of the populist AfD are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation the party strongly rejects.
Its anti-immigration, "Germany first" and Russian-friendly agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east.

Before this week, the last time a US president greeted a foreign leader at Joint Base Andrews was when John F. Kennedy welcomed British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan in 1962.
But thatâs not the reason the image of US President Donald Trump waiting at the foot of the stairs of an Air China Boeing-747 to personally greet Chinese leader Xi Jinping is historic. Macmillan led a close American ally; Xi leads Americaâs paramount adversary. In rolling out the red carpet, Trump underscored how rapidly the balance of power in the relationship has shifted.
The turning point came last year, when China made the ultimate power move, threatening to choke off rare earths â and turn US factories dark â after Trump ramped up tariffs on Chinese goods to more than 140%.
Trump backed down, and at the time, Rush Doshi, a Georgetown University professor and former Biden administration official, wrote that China had proved itself to be a âtrue peerâ of the US, unafraid to push back. Doshiâs take on the arrival ceremony, which also included a 21-gun salute and a flyover by B-1B bombers â far exceeding courtesies extended to Trump in Beijing in May â has been that China believes âtheyâve basically tamed the United States.â
âThe tectonic plates have shifted beneath us,â he told me, âand both leaders are acting accordingly.â
The China scholar Orville Schell writes that the USâ epic diplomatic successes of the 20th century â securing the unconditional surrender of Japan and Germany after World War Two; defusing the Cuban missile crisis; securing arms-control agreements with Moscow to wind down the Cold War â set an unrealistic ceiling for Americans about whatâs achievable today. This summit established a new, lower floor.
In classic diplomacy, protocol giveaways are supposed to be reciprocated by substantive concessions. Otherwise, why bother?
Xi offered two pandas â Ping Ping and Fu Shuang â for the Atlanta zoo, bromides on how the US and China must âcoexist in peaceâ and, according to Trump, showed interest in the granite used to construct the new White House helipad.
Yet at the same time, China is supplying Russia with dual-use technology to pummel Ukraine, and as Xi landed, The Wall Street Journal was reporting details of how Beijing had supplied Iran with rocket propellant and electronic components used to make drones and missiles that Tehran is using to lash out at its neighbors â and reportedly kill US service personnel â in the Gulf.
As for actual results, there was talk of an AI hotline to notify each other of risks that rise to the national security level, and an agreement to extend a trade truce for two months. But again, reality belies the rhetoric: Itâs far from clear that China and the US assess AI risks in the same way â and whether a hotline would actually work. Moreover, the short extension of the trade armistice only underscores its fragility; Beijing is still squeezing flows of rare earths to extract concessions from the US and coerce its allies, including Japan.
Itâs worth remembering that, until quite recently, US and Chinese leaders aired their disagreements in front of TV cameras at joint news conferences on issues ranging from human rights to market access for foreign companies, with American presidents pressing for concessions.
This week, by contrast, has been an exercise in shallow bonhomie. Even a few Republican loyalists have recoiled at the extravagant pageantry, seemingly designed to flatter Xi and awe a domestic audience, although the absence of TV cameras at the Rose Garden ceremony undermined that low-ambition objective. Ahead of the summit, Roger Wicker, the Senate Armed Services Committee Chairman, questioned why Trump was offering such a âlavish welcomeâ to a âbrutal, unelected, and oppressive dictator.â
After a state dinner featuring bok choy and sesame-crusted sea bass â and a clutch of tech moguls including Tim Cook, Elon Musk, and Jensen Huang â the puzzle remains: Why did Trump blow diplomatic capital for such meager results?
âTremendous things will be happening,â Trump posted on Friday. Thatâs a diplomatic hope, not a deliverable.

3dd25706de50.text: By — Kevin Freking, Associated Press Kevin Freking, Associated Press By — Jonathan J. Cooper, Associated Press Jonathan J. Cooper, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-administration-uses-rare-authority-to-claw-back-nearly-1b-in-spending-approved-by-congress Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump administration uses rare authority to claw back nearly $1B in spending approved by Congress Politics Sep 26, 2026 1:20 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump is canceling nearly $1 billion in spending approved by Congress, the White House announced on Friday, using a rare and contested power to axe funding for immigrant services and diversity-focused initiatives. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Trump's Office of Management and Budget described the funding cut as focused on "the most harmful government spending." Most of the cuts are focused on Health and Human Services programs that serve refugees and unaccompanied minors accused of being in the country illegally. The administration says the funds are no longer necessary because illegal border crossings have diminished considerably. Also targeted for cuts were a Department of Education program for migrant students, a Department of Justice office focused on reducing racial tensions, a business development initiative for minority entrepreneurs, housing counseling services from the Housing and Urban Development Department and a series of grants from the Health and Human Services Department that the administration called "outright harmful and blatantly ideological." A White House press release announcing the funding rescissions notes that some of the organizations are led by people who worked in the administration of Democratic President Barack Obama. Trump's move was condemned by Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, a Republican in a tough reelection campaign and chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. Collins said in a statement that the action came without warning or consultation. She also said she would work to address with colleagues "these illegal actions." "Not only is the delay itself an impoundment that was not reported to Congress, but also it is a usurpation of Congress's appropriations powers," Collins said. "OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding." WATCH: House passes short-term spending bill, staving off another fund fight during midterms Under federal law, Congress has 45 days to review the president's proposed spending cuts before they take effect. But Trump made that all but impossible by announcing them with just five days left in the federal fiscal year and the House out of session through the November election. The Government Accountability Office, which is an arm of Congress, says the maneuver known as a "pocket rescission" is illegal. Collins called it the latest attempt by OMB to "undermine Congress's Constitutional power of the purse." A year ago, Trump issued a pocket rescission for the first time in nearly 50 years by blocking $4.9 billion in congressionally approved foreign aid. The U.S. Supreme Court declined to block those rescissions, saying that Trump's authority over foreign affairs weighed heavily in its decision. This year, Trump is targeting domestic spending. The use of a "pocket rescission" fits into a broader pattern by the Trump administration to exert greater control over the U.S. government, eroding Congress's power. What was essentially the last pocket rescission occurred in 1977 when then-Democratic President Jimmy Carter rescinded it, and the Trump administration argues it's a legally permissible tool, despite some murkiness, since Carter had initially proposed the clawback well ahead of the 45-day deadline. The administration has also fired federal workers, imposed a historic increase in tariffs, and started the war in Iran without going through Congress, putting the burden on the judicial branch to determine the limits of presidential power. Sen. Patty Murray of Washington, the lead Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, described the White House action as "theft from the American people, plain and simple." "These are funds Congress has delivered on a bipartisan basis and should be helping people—not cut off by a president more focused on building a ballroom than investing in families," Murray said. Murray said that in recent spending negotiations, Democrats fought to include language to prevent the administration from usurping Congress' power on spending decisions, but Republicans have declined to go along. "While Trump spends tax dollars on ads promoting himself, Congress needs to reassert its powers to help people, and it's past time Republicans join us in that fight," she said. In addition to immigrant services, the White House said it was rescinding $70 million for what it called "woke" international education programs, $28 million in grant funding for Health and Human Services research programs, and $9 million in debt relief for foreign countries that fund climate change policies. Another $10 million was being withheld from a minority business development program. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 463f1be6e502.text: By — Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Nicole Winfield, Associated Press By — Samuel Petrequin, Associated Press Samuel Petrequin, Associated Press By — Sylvie Corbet, Associated Press Sylvie Corbet, Associated Press By — John Leicester, Associated Press John Leicester, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/pope-leo-draws-800000-people-to-central-paris-for-open-air-mass-on-iconic-square Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Pope Leo draws 800,000 people to central Paris for open-air Mass on iconic square World Sep 26, 2026 1:07 PM EDT PARIS (AP) — Hundreds of thousands of people packed Paris' iconic Champs-Élysées avenue to attend an open-air Mass with Pope Leo XIV on Saturday, a sign of the Catholic Church's enduring appeal in the once staunchly Catholic but officially secular country. The Vatican estimated that 800,000 people attended — about 200,000 more than the number who had registered in advance. The turnout testified to the church's lasting influence in France despite declining attendance and secularizing trends that have emptied churches across Europe. The American pope greeted the flag-waving, cheering throngs from his popemobile during a 2-kilometer (1.2-mile) parade along the grand boulevard leading to the Place de la Concorde for Mass, essentially the heart of Paris and a symbol of the French republic. READ MORE: Pope opens France trip with warning that a 'paradise of machines' could undermine humanity In his homily, Leo asked the crowds not to keep their faith to themselves, but to instead "let it overflow, so that those you meet may be refreshed and their thirst satisfied." "From this beautiful city of Paris, I pray fervently that the living water of the Holy Spirit may flow throughout France," he said. Although a security blanket shut down central Paris to road traffic, the party-like atmosphere drew people of multiple faiths and no faith at all. The fervor spanned generations. People brought dozens of babies and young children from the crowd for Leo to caress on the head as he rode slowly past aboard the popemobile. "The message of Pope Leo goes well beyond Catholic people; he speaks about social justice, for example," said Leontine Joseph, 42, a fervent Catholic who came with two friends of Moroccan origin who grew up in Muslim culture. An appeal to persevere against the trends Leo has sought to encourage French Catholics to persevere in their faith "even amid the thorns" of a secular world during his four-day visit. It began on Friday with his arrival and prayer at the restored Notre Dame, the first by a pope since the cathedral's devastating 2019 fire. After Paris, Leo headed for the Catholic shrine at Lourdes. At the Catholic Institute of Paris on Saturday morning, the pope said he was surprised by the number of new converts in recent years. READ MORE: Pope Leo XIV affirms need for media to cover public figures when asked about Trump ban "We must recognize, welcome and protect the small flame that the Holy Spirit has kindled in the darkness of the night, the tiny seed that strives to grow even amid the thorns," he said. Adult baptisms in France each year have tripled since 2016, hitting 13,000 this year. But statistics and experts caution that the uptick, which has also been recorded in secular Spain, doesn't counteract the overall downward trend. In 1980, there were 513,000 baptisms in France; in 2024, a total of 186,000. The pope is a crowd-puller The rivers of people who crammed central Paris and their joyful enthusiasm rivaled other communal but non-religious moments of celebration that marked France in recent decades. Huge crowds celebrated on the Champs-Elysées when France won the soccer World Cup in 1998 and again in 2018. Many on Saturday didn't identify as Catholics, but came to hear the pope's message. "People are seeing a lot of really terrible images. This kind of event reminds people of what is really important in life," said Thierry Chen, a 40-year-old Parisian startup entrepreneur who is not Catholic. "You see a lot of different people here, so it's not just about one race, religion or nation, but about a common belief in humankind." Pope Leo celebrates an open-air Mass at the Place de la Concorde, in Paris, as part of his four-day apostolic journey to France, on Sept. 26, 2026. Photo by Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters Sylvane Le Goff, 68, who lives in the Paris region, came with her 10- and 12-year-old grandchildren to "give them unforgettable memories." Le Goff, who was raised Catholic but is not practicing, said she wanted to open her grandchildren's minds. "It's not only about seeing the pope but it also is about his message of peace and unity, values I'd like to share with them," she said. Leo has clearly been impressed by the numbers and enthusiasm, especially at a Friday night vigil that kept the 71-year-old pope out until nearly 11 p.m. after a packed first day. Some 80,000 young people filled the national stadium for an extravaganza of fireworks and a theatrical retelling of French Catholic history. "Thank you for your courage! Thank you for your presence," Leo said to raucous cheers, speaking off the cuff in French. "Thank you for your faith. You are the saints of France!" Mass adds a new chapter for historic Paris square The imposing stage erected for the Mass, capped with a golden cross, and rows upon rows of choir singers, clergy and others who prayed under the pope's gaze on Place de la Concorde marked a new chapter for the history-steeped square. It was an execution site during the French Revolution. Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette were guillotined there. For many in France, it embodies the Republic and traditionally stages Bastille Day celebrations. In 2024, the Paris Olympics gave it a blast of modernity, using it for break dance, skateboard, BMX and 3X3 basketball events.
