Food Safety Finds a Place Among ‘Kitchen-Table’ Political Issues
The run-up to the midterm elections is turning into a food fight — literally.
The summer was marred by a massive foodborne outbreak that sickened scores of people and the recall of tens of thousands of pounds of imported meat, turning the safety of the U.S. food supply into a topic of national conversation and a political cause.
Late-night talk show hosts joked about symptoms that included explosive diarrhea. As a precaution, chain restaurants such as Chipotle and Taco Bell yanked lettuce, jalapeños, and other suspected products from menus. Some food safety scientists blamed the outbreaks on federal cuts to public health.
These dynamics collectively have raised questions about whether it’s safe to order a salad or burger.
Democrats have come out on the offensive, saying voters worried about the safety of the U.S. food supply should oust Republicans in the midterm elections. The Trump administration has countered by accusing Democrats of scaremongering over food safety to score political points.
The political fracas reflects the toll that large-scale outbreaks have had on the public psyche. Midterm voters have long cared about pocketbook issues such as grocery prices, but the spate of recalls has them worried about whether the food they’re buying is safe to eat — and political leaders are paying attention.
The outbreak linked to cyclospora in lettuce led to almost 20,000 laboratory-confirmed cases of illness from May through August, compared with 1,180 cases during the same span in 2025, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That makes it the largest recorded outbreak of the parasite.
“One of the reasons food safety is in the news this year, and people have been rightfully concerned, is the combination of high-profile restaurant names and the absolute colossal number of illnesses,” said Teresa Murray, consumer watchdog director with the U.S. Public Interest Research Group, or PIRG, an advocacy group, referring to a recent cyclosporiasis outbreak. “It’s thousands of people. It makes it more real.”
Data shows there have been about 200 food recalls so far in 2026, which is about on par with the number at this time last year, according to PIRG data.
Following the Numbers
A majority of registered voters have little or no confidence in government oversight of food safety, with Democrats far more likely than Republicans to doubt the protections in place, according to a July survey by Quinnipiac University. Ninety-four percent of U.S. adults indicated they were concerned about the frequency of food recalls in a poll by GS1 US, a data standards organization.
The share of consumers who strongly agree that the U.S. food system produces food that’s safe to eat declined to about 30% in August, from 40% in November, based on survey data released in September by the University of Illinois and Purdue University.
Democrats have jumped at the chance to repeat criticisms of President Donald Trump’s budget cuts and priorities.
The Democratic National Committee recently posted a list of recalled food items on social media while calling Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. a “complete disaster” who must resign.
“Trump is dismantling our government — and it’s harming people,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) posted Sept. 2 on the social platform X, adding: “Slashed food safety agencies → cyclospora outbreak.” Just weeks earlier, she had written to Kennedy demanding answers for what she described as the administration’s “failed response” and its connection to political contributions.
Rep. Gabe Amo (D-R.I.) posted Sept. 5 on X: “I’m calling on Trump to stop gutting the FDA & restore its inspectors. We deserve safe food.”
The campaign for Rep. Judy Chu (D-Calif.) posted Sept. 5 on X: “Trump is cutting our food safety funding and workforce, and we have seen far too many food recalls this summer.”
But the number of recalls doesn’t tell the whole story.
While recalls aren’t markedly up this year compared with 2025, they are up over a broader time span. The country saw 320 food recalls by the Food and Drug Administration and the U.S. Department of Agriculture in 2025, up from 296 in 2024, according to PIRG.
The total number of recalls grew 21% from 2021 to 2025, based on an analysis by Trace One, a provider of regulatory guidance software. A rise in Class I recalls, which are the highest priority because the products could cause serious illness or death, drove much of the increase.
But recall numbers can be misleading. For starters, federal agencies do not publicize all recalls, especially if products are no longer on the market. Recall data itself is suspect because a single contaminated food can result in multiple recalls if the item is incorporated into processed food or other products.
A far better measure is the number of people sickened, epidemiologists say. And this summer’s specific multistate outbreak from cyclospora was exceptional, affecting people in 21 states.
When it comes to bacterial contamination of food — which is more common and includes E. coli, listeria, and salmonella — the overall trend points to outbreaks in which fewer people are falling ill. That’s a promising sign, some food safety leaders say, although the CDC says an estimated 48 million people each year in the U.S. experience foodborne illness.
“That’s an indication we’re finding more outbreaks and finding more when they are smaller and limiting the extent to which they can get bigger,” said Craig Hedberg, a public health professor at the University of Minnesota and leader in food safety surveillance.
Still, the perception that the food supply is riskier has been enough to ignite political rancor.

The extreme heat scientists have warned about for decades came to Europe again this summer, killing at least 30,000 people like a silent, invisible plague. It came for poor people, the very young and very old, and those suffering from debilitating conditions.
The final toll will likely be higher. A 2024 United Nations report estimated about 175,000 annual heat-related deaths across Europe, and total deaths in European Union countries spiked above 60,000 in 2022 and 2024.
The heat started earlier than ever, in late May, and kept coming in deadly, unrelenting waves that destroyed crops and vineyards, buckled railroad tracks, turned forests to kindling and dried up rivers and lakes. When it settled heavily over Bologna, Italy, in late June, residents of the industrial region said it was like a stifling, life-threatening force that you feel in your bones, transforming streets and buildings into radiators blasting warmth day and night, making routine outdoor chores dangerous.
Heat is hard to see, but you feel it in the pavement, in the walls of poorly insulated apartments, in sweat that never quite dries and a bedroom that just won’t cool down. And people do not experience it equally.
Bologna photographer Michele Lapini made those differences visible, using his iPhone and a thermal sensor to document temperatures in homes, workplaces and public spaces as the heat gripped the city. The images show that construction workers in direct sun, delivery riders crossing the city and residents of old apartment buildings and poorly cooled senior centers inhabit radically different thermal worlds than people with access to air conditioning, shade and well-insulated homes.
Lapini said he felt a great sense of resignation as he talked with people about the heat. What could they do? They had no choice but to work. They couldn’t move or get a permit to install air conditioning, or afford it. The problem sometimes feels too large to solve individually, and he said he felt that recently as he tried to decide whether to install air conditioning, knowing that it would make the overall problem worse.
Federico Grazzini, a Bologna-based expert with the regional meteorological service, said the daytime high temperatures in the summer of 2026 made it stand out from other recent extreme summers, including 2003. The 2026 heat was also notable for its persistence, “with five major heatwaves, at least a week long,” separated by only short cool spells.
In Bologna, the central downtown weather station recorded 81 tropical nights, of which 24 were “equatorial nights,” with temperatures staying above 77 degrees Fahrenheit, and there were 52 “scorching days,” with daytime highs above 95 degrees Fahrenheit.
Grazzini said 2026 “represented a landmark year in people’s perception of the climatic crisis,” as the heat became one of the main topics in daily discourse. But he faulted Italian mainstream media for not explaining the links between global warming and the heat. “In most cases,” he said, “they fail to convey the large picture behind the chronicle and drama of the single events.”
Lapini’s images capture the thermal tension running through Bologna’s cityscape. What looks like a Europe-wide heatwave through satellite sensors becomes something much more unequal at street level. Staying out of deadly heat can depend on whether you own or rent a home, whether your building has been renovated and whether you have access to trees, shade or a public place where you can escape the heat.
“Thermal comfort should not be a luxury,” said Eleni Myrivili, global chief heat officer with the United Nations Environmental Programme. On a planet wracked by human-caused warming, protection from extreme heat is a necessity for “health, dignity, productivity and increasingly, for survival.”
Myrivili was elected to the Athens, Greece, city council in 2014, served as deputy mayor for resilience and climate adaptation and later became the city’s first chief heat officer in 2021, the first such position in Europe at the time.
At an online briefing on extreme heat in early September, she said cities struggle to develop and implement heat protection measures because the pace of climate impacts is accelerating. And city governments are often hampered by fragmented politics, limited capacity and financing. The decisions needed to make cities safer, from retrofitting buildings to expanding shade and green space, “often do not bring votes,” she said.
Elected officials can “put their heads in the sand” because voters don’t hold them responsible for providing solutions, she said. Central European cities and countries, she added, have the resources to protect people, but need the political courage to use them.
Lapini said his images reveal how political decisions, as well as inaction,can have unfair consequences. He said that, as he documented thermal injustice, he realized that climate policies need to start with the communities and people most affected. And it’s impossible to make effective climate laws, he said, without considering the economic and political structures that produced the climate crisis.
The photographs were taken in Bologna between June 22 and July 7.
About This Story
Perhaps you noticed: This story, like all the news we publish, is free to read. That’s because Inside Climate News is a 501c3 nonprofit organization. We do not charge a subscription fee, lock our news behind a paywall, or clutter our website with ads. We make our news on climate and the environment freely available to you and anyone who wants it.
That’s not all. We also share our news for free with scores of other media organizations around the country. Many of them can’t afford to do environmental journalism of their own. We’ve built bureaus from coast to coast to report local stories, collaborate with local newsrooms and co-publish articles so that this vital work is shared as widely as possible.

Senate Democrats led by Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., are pressing Secretary of State Marco Rubio to intervene as renewed fighting in the Tigray region of Ethiopia raises fears of a return to the 2020-2022 civil war. In a statement shared first with Semafor, the senators warn that the African Union-brokered deal ending that war, an agreement Washington backed, is âunraveling.â The group of senators â which includes all Democratic members of the Senate Foreign Relations Committeeâs Africa panel â criticized both sides of the conflict. They condemned a drone strike on a truck carrying US-funded food aid for displaced people in northwestern Tigray in which the Ethiopian military is suspected, and accused the Tigrayan forces of undermining the regionâs interim government, refusing to disarm, and forcibly conscripting civilians. They also faulted the Trump administration for letting sanctions on regional actors lapse days before hostilities resumed.
â Adrian Elimian
Know More
Tensions in Tigray have escalated for months with clashes and airstrikes. Last week, the Tigray Peopleâs Liberation Front declared a âdefensive warâ before its forces seized key locations and pushed into neighboring Afar and Amhara regions. Just days before, the TPLF publicly allied with other Ethiopian armed groups aiming to overthrow the federal government.
The renewed conflict has heightened fears of further destabilization in a volatile region beset by other conflicts in Sudan, Somalia, and Yemen. The 2020-2022 Tigray war killed more than 100,000 people and contributed to famine in the region.
Washingtonâs approach has been mixed. The administration imposed sanctions in June on unnamed TPLF officials it said were undermining peace, but let the 2021 executive order behind the broader Ethiopia sanctions program expire this month. The State Department condemned the aid convoy strike without naming who was responsible.

The News
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is running into a wall of congressional GOP resistance as he tries to secure $1.5 trillion for the Pentagon next year.
Lawmakersâ growing reluctance to fulfill Hegsethâs eye-popping budget request reflects real intraparty concerns about his leadership, his relationship with Congress, and the ongoing war with Iran. It also punctuates months of drama at the Pentagon over the ouster and resignation of various top officials, in addition to reports of blocked military promotions.
Hegsethâs fraying ties on the Hill put him on course for a bigger headache after the election, according to interviews with a half-dozen senators as well as multiple administration officials.
âThis could turn into a real standoff with the military caught in the middle,â a Trump administration official told Semafor. âThe implications: There wonât be money available to pay recruitment bonuses, money to upgrade military housing and repair military housing wonât be there, money to fix ships and aircraft from the war wonât be there, and money to restockpile munitions wonât be there.
âAnd the longer this drags out, the more dangerous it becomes, because weâre really depleted after the Iran war,â the official added.
Hegseth is pushing for both a sharp increase in military funding â heâs seeking spending more than 40% higher than last year â and a separate $88 billion to cover costs associated with the Iran war and additional weapons. The Pentagon chiefâs expansive needs only heighten some Republicansâ skepticism of his leadership over the US military.
It does not appear that Hegseth has an executable plan to get the hundreds of billions in additional military funding he is requesting in the fall, one Republican senator told Semafor, adding that the lack of permanent civilian nominees to lead the Army and Navy are weighing on the Senate. Hegsethâs preferred pick for Army secretary, Sean Parnell, has faced questions over whether he could even be confirmed by the GOP Senate.
âThere are a lot of people that are really upset with the war in Iran and how itâs being played out. We feel itâs hurting our chances in the elections in the fall, and it seems rather haphazard,â said the senator.
âWe donât like what weâre seeing when it comes to the pulling of officers off of the promotion lists,â this senator added. âWe donât like what we see with â¦ indiscriminate firings of admirals and generals across the force.â
Hegseth retains the backing of President Donald Trump, despite his Republican doubters in Congress. Those closest to Trump currently see no chance that Hegseth is replaced. That would leave GOP lawmakers with little choice but to work with him, lest they risk holding up funding the White House says is badly needed.
âThe president still is very much in Peteâs corner, but beneath him, there are very serious concerns,â the Trump official said. âAre they going to be able to get any additional money through? Are they going to be able to get any nominees confirmed?â
Most Republicans believe a party-line budget reconciliation bill is the best way to get the Pentagon more money after the election. But getting 50 out of the 53 GOP senators on board for that would be a major challenge.
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who regrets voting to confirm Hegseth, said the secretaryâs quandary âcomes down to relationships, and I donât think heâs built strong enough relationships.â Tillis said the first âmeaningful briefingâ heâs received on Iran occurred last week; the senator subsequently voted against continuing the war, along with three Republican colleagues.
Those four senators alone would be enough to tank a party-line defense spending bill. And given Hegsethâs distance from Congress, Tillis asked Semafor, âwhy is anybody going to blindly appropriate anything to him?â
âI agree thereâs friction,â said Sen. John Kennedy, R-La. âThe genesis of that friction is different, depending upon the senator.â
The Trump administration canât rely on Democrats to pass bipartisan legislation if multiple Republicans are already set to block Hegsethâs request. The secretary, as the administration official noted, is ânot going to get Democrat votes â he just canât do it.â
Kennedy agreed: âAnybody who thinks that weâre going to get money for the Pentagon, which needs it, other than through reconciliation, needs to put down the bong.â He urged Republicans âto sit down and talk about it.â
Hegsethâs supporters also acknowledge a rift thatâs damaging the Pentagonâs ability to get what it wants. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said in an interview that the continued lack of engagement with Democrats âcontinues to be a strategic errorâ for Hegseth and his team.
âRepublicans are frustrated that he hasnât reached out to Democrats. He didnât in his confirmation, and he hasnât much since at all,â Cramer said.
Kingsley Wilson, a spokesperson for the Pentagon, said the administration conducted over 500 briefings on the budget request â some of them bipartisan â and said the department is âin lockstep with the Republican conference in Congress to achieve the Presidentâs historic investment in defense.â
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
Know More
At the heart of the GOP frustration with Hegseth is his handling of military firings and promotions. Cramer supports much of what the secretary has done but acknowledged the turbulence has âbothered some people.
âAnd it probably has had an impact on morale a little bit,â Cramer added. âBut all in all, I think Peteâs a pretty strong leader.â
Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, worked to arrange a bipartisan classified briefing about the administrationâs funding request last week. The Senate Armed Services Committee also heard closed testimony from Hegsethâs top deputies, including Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg.
But Collins is cool to another party-line bill. âI donât like reconciliation, period,â she told Semafor â and Hegseth, who she voted against.

On Monday, China released more information of what was agreed at the talks between Xi Jinping and Donald Tump last week, shedding light on a handful of concrete outcomes.
But there were no joint statements and few major breakthroughs.
Instead, both governments issued separate accounts of the meeting - perhaps a sign that despite the White House tours and promise of warmer ties, Washington and Beijing remain wary of each other.
Here are four things we now know - and still don't - about what transpired at the talks.
A new AI dialogue and communication channel
Beijing says it has agreed with Washington to launch a new AI dialogue, with further talks scheduled for the end of November.
As both countries race to develop advanced artificial intelligence, the move suggests they see a need for some guardrails around a technology that is increasingly being used in everything from business to military planning.
They have also agreed to establish a communication channel for AI-related incidents, aimed at preventing misunderstandings or unexpected developments from turning into a broader confrontation.
The meeting was being closely watched for any developments or agreements in relation to AI - especially in the wake of calls by US companies like Anthropic to slow down developments, and revelations that Open AI had gained unauthorised access to government websites in countries like Australia and had "meddled" with multiple US government agency sites.
Trade truce - what was included and what was left out
Chinese state media confirmed for the first time on Monday that the trade truce has been extended until 10 January.
The short extension ensures both leaders will meet again at major international gatherings later this year.
Trump will attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November while Xi is due to travel to Miami for the G20 summit in December.
It is rare for the leaders of the world's two largest economies to meet so frequently.
But Beijing had hoped for a much longer extension to the truce, making the two month reprieve a modest gain rather than a major breakthrough.
China did secure lower tariffs on $30bn (Â£23bn) of goods entering the US with reciprocal reductions expected from Beijing.
Chinese products heading to American stores ranging from toys to small household appliances to Christmas decorations will benefit from the lower tariffs.
The Trump administration also said Beijing would buy at least 10 million metric tons of coal annually in 2027 and 2028.
What is striking is what was left out.
There was no mention of increasing exports of China's rare earth minerals to the US nor was there any indication that restrictions on advanced US semiconductors would be eased.
The US left out Taiwan - but China didn't
The White House factsheet made no mention of Taiwan, but the issue was clearly a priority for Xi Jinping.
According to Beijing's accounts of the talks, Xi urged Donald Trump to formally oppose Taiwan independence and handle the issue with caution.
After their previous meeting in May, Trump revealed that Xi directly asked him if the US would defend Taiwan in the event of a Chinese attack.
He told reporters, "There's only one person that knows that, and it is me," and he raised the question whether it made sense for US forces to "travel 9,500 miles to fight a war" over the issue.
This time, Trump disclosed far less.
"We didn't talk about it too much," he told reporters over the weekend.
"Right now, it's fine. It's just moving along," Trump said. "He understands very much how I feel."
That silence may be significant.
Trump has previously described a proposed $14bn US arms package for Taiwan as "a very good negotiating chip" in his dealings with Beijing. The arms package has been on hold for months.
Adding to the confusion, US Ambassador to China David Perdue told Fox News that Trump had offered to sell weapons to Xi during the summit.
The State Department later clarified that US law prohibits arms sales to China and there are no plans to do so.
Beijing sees the self-governing island as part of China. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.
China may be opening the investment doors
China says it will allow more foreign financial firms, including American-backed banks, investment companies and insurers, to apply to do business and open offices in China. But any approvals will still be subject to Chinese laws and regulations.
The last line is key. China is opening the door, but still controls who gets through it.
Foreign financial firms have long complained that regulatory barriers, licensing requirements and concerns over exit bans make it difficult to expand in China, even when market access is technically allowed.
Beijing also said it was discussing ways to increase the number of flights between both countries, but neither side has explained how this would happen.
And despite giving visa free entry to visitors from more than 75 countries across the world, China has not extended that offer to Americans.
Meanwhile the US State Department continues to classify travel to China as a Level 2 advisory urging travellers to "exercise increased caution" because of the risk of arbitrary law enforcement, exit bans and detention.
So even though both sides are talking about encouraging business and travel some of the biggest obstacles remain firmly in place.
So what do we know?
This summit produced more dialogue - but very little decision change for now. The most contentious issues from advanced technology to Taiwan remain unresolved.
But for both leaders, this is a familiar outcome - a promise of more channels of communication, modest economic concessions and modest proposals to steady relations.
And while both remain committed to a steady relationship - continued US-China dialogue appears far easier

This story is a collaboration between Inside Climate News and Honolulu Civil Beat.
All over Hawaiʻi, property owners are hoping to rebuild homes and businesses destroyed by recent disasters.
Many Kauaʻi and Hawaiʻi island residents are still assessing the damage caused by downed trees and utility poles or cleaning the mud and sewage that flooded their homes during Hurricane Lowell this month and Hurricane Lala last month. On Oʻahu, Maui and Molokaʻi, homeowners are in various stages of rebuilding properties that were destroyed during back-to-back Kona low storms in March and the deadly 2023 wildfires.
Recovery is already an uphill battle, but too often it brings another hazard: scams.
“We all like to think, as we’re born and raised in Hawai’i, that that local aloha spirit is there, that people will genuinely always be good to you because you’re in a bad position, but that’s not the reality,” said state Sen. Angus McKelvey, who lost his home in the Lahaina fire.
Home repair and contractor scams proliferate after natural disasters. Since the Lahaina fire, dozens of people have contacted local and state officials about serious problems with their contractors. But more than three years after the disaster, officials have filed no criminal charges against contractors for post-wildfire misconduct, and state regulators said they did not believe that any licenses had been revoked, a Civil Beat and Inside Climate News investigation found earlier this month.
Because climate change is expected to ramp up the frequency and intensity of natural disasters, residents everywhere should know how to protect themselves from contractor fraud and other common post-disaster scams.
“Education is so key,” said Heidi Ho, executive director of a Maui-based legal nonprofit formed in the wake of the 2023 disaster to provide free legal advice to the community. “At least now we can hopefully get ahead of it.”
Ho and her organization, PONO Legal, are working with community organizers and officials on Kauaʻi and Hawaiʻi island to support residents affected by recent disasters there. Addressing scams and fraud after the fact is difficult, so Ho said she hopes other islands can learn from survivors’ experience on Maui and increase public awareness before it’s too late.
Maui County Prosecutor Andrew Martin and other officials emphasized that anyone can fall victim to contractor fraud or other scams, and it is not something to feel embarrassed or ashamed about. Local and state law enforcement officials have been working to hold contractors accountable for harming homeowners, Martin said, but filing criminal charges related to fraud and scams can take a long time. He urged homeowners to report all instances of suspected fraud and take steps to reduce the odds of being scammed.
“It’s every professional’s responsibility to follow the law, to be licensed and engage in good business practices,” Martin said. “But I also want to make sure that people are able to protect themselves against the bad actors, because they’re out there.”
Hiʻilei Casco, a staff attorney at PONO Legal, urged homeowners to trust their gut and pay attention to concerns about contractors, even if they’re in the middle of a build. If something seems to be going wrong, they should withhold payment until the issue is resolved, Casco said.
“No concern is too small in these types of situations, especially after disasters where exploitation is much higher,” she said. “Homeowners’ funds are their greatest leverage.”
What Can I Do to Protect Myself?
Document everything: After a disaster hits, be sure to take photos and videos of any damage before you begin cleanup so you can show your insurance company the full scope of damage, like flooding or rubble. Continue to document throughout the rebuilding. If you are having problems with your contractor, don’t just call them. Explain your complaints and describe any incorrect or substandard work in texts or emails, and save these communications. They will be helpful if you have to file official reports.
Be wary of solicitors: Scammers often come to you to offer their services. They may approach you on your property or after identifying you as a potential target following a community meeting, or they may reach out to you over the phone or by email.
Get estimates from multiple contractors and your insurer: If an offer seems too good to be true, it probably is.
Ask for and verify customer references: Negligent or nefarious contractors may tell you that they have worked with specific people or share photographs of projects they claim to have completed. Don’t take their word for it. Check up on those claims.
Research your contractor: You can use the state Department of Commerce and Consumer Affairs “Business Check” website to make sure a contractor is licensed, in good standing and insured to protect you from liability if an accident occurs on your property. You may be able to read reviews for contracting companies online and on the Better Business Bureau website, but scammers may frequently change their business’ name, so also search on the name of the business owner, the business’ filing address or its phone number, along with terms like “review,” “scam” and “complaint.”
Get agreements in writing and scrutinize the terms: Before signing a contract, read it carefully and consult a lawyer, case manager or other expert if you can (some organizations like PONO Legal offer these consults for free). Contracts are required by state law to include details such as the work to be performed, total costs and the projected start and completion dates. Never sign a contract that does not specify the total dollar amount or that has blank spaces to be filled in later. The contract should also include information about subcontractors and the homeowner’s lien rights, which will protect you if the contractor fails to pay their workers.
Be careful when making payments: Do not offer personal financial information over the phone or use reloadable d

4060f8d4183a.text: Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) is launching a six-week campaign blitz that will take him to more than 40 congressional districts across 22 states through Election Day, Axios has learned. Why it matters: Johnson is going all-in on defending Republicans' House majority at a moment when the political terrain is shifting toward Democrats. The Cook Political Report moved 15 House races toward Democrats on Friday and said Republicans would need to win a majority of the remaining toss-up races to keep control of the chamber. Driving the news: Johnson's campaign swing will be split evenly between Republican-held seats the party is fighting to defend and Democratic-held districts the GOP hopes to pick up, according to details shared first with Axios. The speaker begins his travel this week in Louisiana and New York. He'll also campaign in Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas, Virginia, Washington, and Wisconsin. The six-week sprint builds on Johnson's August road show, when he traveled across 18 states for 75 events in 52 cities. What they're saying: "With less than 40 days until the most consequential midterm election in modern history, Republicans are not slowing down as we give voters a clear choice between common sense and Democrats' crazy," Johnson told Axios in a statement. "From coast to coast, I am leaving it all on the field to defend our House majority because the stakes have never been higher. Democrats have embraced socialism and communism and nominated the most radical candidates to ever run for Congress," the speaker continued. Zoom out: Johnson has also broken fundraising records, raising more through the second quarter than any Republican speaker or leader in a midterm cycle. Earlier this month, Johnson announced another $13 million transfer to GOP incumbents, challengers and the NRCC. The NRCC enters the final stretch with $13 million more cash on hand than the DCCC, the largest lead the committee has ever held at this point in the election cycle.

Governor VÃctor Manuel Castro CosÃo said temporary shelters had been opened should residents need to be evacuated.
The federal authorities have also deployed thousands of members of the navy and the army along with specialised machinery.

An offshore wind turbine facility is to be created at the Port of Montrose, supporting about 80 jobs.
The factory, which will make components for off-shore wind turbines, is to be run by engineering firm Subsea Micropiles following a Â£5m investment.
A further Â£6.7m is being provided by the state-owned Scottish National Investment Bank, with Scottish Enterprise also pledging Â£1.45m.
First Minister John Swinney, during a visit to the site in Angus, said it would help ensure "benefits of the energy transition are retained in Scotland".
He also welcomed an announcement from SSE that the Port of Montrose is its preferred location for an operations base for the Berwick Bank B offshore wind farm, which is expected to create a further 100 jobs.
The Berwick project, set to be one of the largest offshore wind farms in the world, will see up to 307 turbines generating enough electricity to power up to six million homes.
Scotland 'at the forefront' of offshore energy
Subsea Micropiles, which has offices in Ireland and Aberdeenshire, already has an operations base at the Port of Montrose.
The firm's new facility is expected to make parts for wind turbines in Scottish waters, and for international markets.
Chief executive Derek Robertson said: "Scotland has become an important base for our growth.
"We rely on the deep pool of talent, skills and offshore experience here to develop our technology, services and expand into a global market.
He added that the company's products "can be manufactured locally, with the potential to retain significant economic benefit in Scotland through engineering, vessel services and offshore supply chain".
Swinney said: "Scotland is already recognised as being at the forefront of floating offshore wind development.
"The investment behind today's announcements is a strong vote of confidence in the sector and in the skilled workforce, innovation and expertise that exists here.
"Subsea Micropiles' commitment to expand at the Port of Montrose will help ensure more of the economic benefits of the energy transition are retained in Scotland, creating high-quality jobs in Angus and the North East, supporting local businesses and strengthening our industrial capabilities."
He added that SSE's selection of Montrose as its preferred location for the Berwick project would strengthen "Scotland's offshore wind supply chain" and create "more jobs as well as investment in skills, infrastructure and local communities".

7574bf99e050.text: AI companies, private equity firms and unions are looking beyond 2026 in the data center debate , banding together to form a new multimillion-dollar coalition to make the case for responsible growth in seven key states. Why it matters: The new group, the American Infrastructure Alliance, wants to partner with state and local officials to create standards and guardrails for data centers in 2027. In return, the coalition hopes to head off moratoriums on new construction. The group is planning initial campaigns in Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa, Pennsylvania, Indiana and South Carolina. The alliance is backed by Blackstone, OpenAI, QTS and SoftBank Group, along with key unions, including the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW). What they're saying: "Responsible growth requires clear expectations for everyone involved," said Tag Greason, co-CEO of QTS, the Blackstone-owned data center operator. "Blanket bans on necessary infrastructure projects would set back our economy and threaten good middle-class jobs," said Kenneth Cooper, the IBEW's international president. "The IBEW is committed to responsible development that benefits workers, communities and our nation." "We are proud to join this coalition to chart a clear path forward, so that UA members can continue to protect the health of the nation," said Mark McManus, general president of the United Association of Union Plumbers and Pipefitters (UA) . Between the lines: This isn't an outside group built to flood the airwaves in key congressional races or battleground states ahead of the 2026 midterms. Instead, it represents an initial investment in a broader battle over AI and data centers that will likely bleed into the 2027 state legislative battles and the 2028 presidential campaign. "Texas shouldn't choose between protecting what matters and building what's next," the narrator says in one of its ads , which makes an appeal to Gov. Greg Abbott (R). "We can do both." Zoom out: Data centers have become a defining issue in the 2026 midterm elections, with Democrats hammering Republicans in key states for supporting them. Leading progressives, including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), have unveiled legislation to pause all new data center construction nationwide until AI safeguards are in place. At the state level, Abbott — a cheerleader for data centers before the political backlash to them began — halted approvals for new data centers in early August. A few weeks later, he said data center companies had "dug their own grave" and deserved the backlash they were facing. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) had a similar reversal: Last year he celebrated a $20 billion Amazon investment, but last month signed an executive order to tighten the rules for data center development. Zoom in: Unions are heavily represented in the group, with the goal of activating their members to help convince state and local officials that data centers can be built responsibly. Besides the IBEW, the International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail and Transportation Workers (SMART), the International Association of Heat and Frost Insulators and Allied Workers (HFIAW), the International Association of Iron Workers, and the United Association of Union Plumbers and Pipefitters (UA) are aboard. The group's own polling found that data centers are deeply unpopular in Ohio, with 67% of those surveyed holding an unfavorable opinion, compared with 18% who have a favorable impression. But those numbers flip when data centers pledge to keep electricity costs low, create jobs and generate tax revenue, according to the group's polling. The bottom line: The group wants to work with local officials — not against them. "American workers and communities should have a seat at the table as this critical infrastructure is built," said Michael Coleman, general president of SMART.

The News
Talks over a deal that would see the US help develop Kenyaâs critical minerals processing industry are at a âvery advancedâ stage, the African countryâs mining minister told Semafor, as the nation looks to increase miningâs contribution to its economy.
The talks come against the backdrop of intensifying rivalry between âthe US and China over access to critical minerals.
Hassan Ali Joho said discussions with US government officials were over the creation of refineries and processing plants in Kenya that partly supply the US. âSeveral departments of the US [government] are involved in the discussion,â he said in an interview, specifically referencing the US departments of commerce, defense, and state. âOff-taker discussions are ongoing, several products, several markets, several different interests.âÂ
The ministerâs comments come weeks after a senior American official said the US was ready to help Kenya to develop its local mineral processing.
Asked about the likely operating environment in Kenya as part of an agreement, Joho â minister for mining, blue economy, and maritime affairs â said: âThere has to be all the necessary incentives that the government will provide, such as special economic zones, port access, support infrastructure, and tax concessions.â
Joho said discussions about a critical mineral partnership were âintertwinedâ with the bidding process to develop Mrima Hill, a coastal deposit that is expected to contain tens of billions of dollarsâ worth of rare earth minerals.
He said initial geological studies suggested niobium, a metal used in aerospace manufacturing, is present in Mrima Hill. He added that early stage assessments indicated cobalt, copper, and nickel were also present in Kenya
Know More
Joho said six companies were competing in the bidding process for the Mrima Hill project, including American firms and others from Australia and China. He said the bidding process would end in late October, after which the government would hold talks with a preferred company and agree on a deal.
The mining minister said the sector currently contributes around 1% of Kenyaâs GDP, but that the government was targeting a 10% contribution within the next decade.
âWe are diversifying: we have been a service economy, we have been an agro economy; but now we are keen on opening up the mining sector,â said Joho, adding that the processing materials locally offered the opportunity to drive industrialization and generate wealth among Kenyans.
Step Back
Washington has announced agreements with several African countries â including DR Congo, Nigeria, and Zambia â aimed at securing access to minerals it deems critical to its economic interests. The move comes amid intensifying rivalry with China, which dominates global supply chains for minerals needed for data center construction, defense equipment, and the energy transition.â
Governments across Africa are prioritizing local value addition instead of raw minerals exports and are focused on improving processing capacity.
Kenyaâs President William Ruto has made wealth creation through industrialization a focal point in his pitch to voters ahead of polls next year in which he will seek a second term.
Ruto this month ordered Tata Chemicals to âpack up and leaveâ the country. He accused the company, which exports soda ash, of failing to process minerals locally to make glass and create jobs. The presidentâs comments came weeks after Joho ordered the Indian chemicals company to suspend operations at one of its plants due an alleged failure to meet regulatory requirements, which the firm has denied. Joho said the government remained in talks with Tata Chemicals about âcompliance issuesâ that would determine the companyâs future in the country. The mining minister said the government was likely to open up a bidding process within the next six months for other companies to operate in Kenya with a focus on processing. âI want to see fine glass produced in-country,â he said. âI want to see the soda ash feed into our industries from our own resources. So the conversation largely is about value addition.
Notable
- The US needs a more strategic approach to unlocking private investment opportunities in critical minerals across Africa to avoid âfalling behind on securing long-term economic prosperity,â warned a recent report by the Brookings think tank.

96b8cb8509da.text: By — Leah Willingham, Associated Press Leah Willingham, Associated Press By — John Seewer, Associated Press John Seewer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/powerful-noreaster-floods-northeast-again-causing-problems-from-new-jersey-to-new-england Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Powerful nor'easter floods Northeast again, causing problems from New Jersey to New England Nation Sep 28, 2026 8:21 AM EDT BOSTON (AP) — Residents of coastal communities in the Northeast slogged through floodwaters for a second day as a powerful nor'easter pummeled the shoreline Sunday, knocking out power to tens of thousands of homes. Tidal surges swamped low-lying neighborhoods in New Jersey while wind gusts toppled trees on New York's Long Island, damaging homes and bringing down utility poles. READ MORE: Persistent nor'easter batters U.S. Northeast, causing coastal flooding, outages and at least 1 death In the New Jersey beach town of Sea Bright, each high tide brought a new round of flooding. "It's not like a one-time occurrence," said Caroline Virenius, whose garage filled with about a foot of water (30 centimeters). "It's getting wet again and again." The slow-moving storm, which killed a New York City Housing Authority worker when a tree fell Saturday, was expected to linger through Sunday with heavy rain, strong winds and dangerous surf all the way to New England. Extreme amounts of rain — more than 4 inches (10 centimeters) since Friday in some spots in New Jersey — combined with a surging ocean led to flooding amounts not seen for close to a decade in places used to dealing with high water, residents said. The National Weather Service predicted the storm will weaken over Sunday night with local heavy rain in parts of New England and the mid-Atlantic. But local officials in New Jersey and New York told residents that high tide late Monday could potentially bring more flooding. "There is another band of the storm, a weaker band, but still another band that could hit early this afternoon and later into the evening," said New York's Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman. Nor'easter disrupts flights and utilities The nor'easter triggered memories of Superstorm Sandy, which left behind over $60 billion in damage across the eastern U.S. in 2012. While this storm's impact has been nowhere near that, it could be the first of several along the East Coast this fall because of an El Niño climate pattern that's disrupting this year's weather. Images of waves crashing into sea walls and onto beaches raised concerns about coastal erosion. Well over 100,000 customers were without power across the Northeast and mid-Atlantic at times on Sunday, according to PowerOutage.us. The most widespread outages were in counties along the coast from New Jersey to Connecticut. READ MORE: Where have all the Atlantic hurricanes gone? El Niño might bring record slow storm season Numerous flights were canceled or delayed up and down the coast. More than 250 flights had been canceled at Boston Logan International Airport by late Sunday morning as wind gusts reached 40 mph (64 kph), according to the Massachusetts Port Authority. Flooding the biggest concern from nor'easter The worst of the remaining rainfall was expected Sunday from northern New Jersey into southern New England. While the storm was gradually weakening, tidal flooding would stay through high-tide cycles Sunday night, said Bob Oravec, a lead forecaster with the National Weather Service in College Park, Maryland. In New York City, water a few inches deep filled streets in the Howard Beach neighborhood but didn't deter residents from venturing out for coffee Sunday morning. Carole Ann Palmer, who owns Jingles Bait and Tackle in North Beach Haven, New Jersey, said this was the worst flooding she's seen in 10 years. "Yesterday, I was like, oh my God, it just keeps getting higher and higher," said Palmer, who lives above the store. The front step was swept away in the storm and she saw neighbors kayaking through the streets on Saturday. Her biggest problem on Sunday was taking her two puppies outside to relieve themselves. She had to put on waders and carry them to dry land. "I take one at the time, carry them across the street so they can do their business and then come back, dry them off and then do the other one. It's a workout," Palmer said. New Jersey community better prepared after Sandy Bernard Dowd waded through tidal water Sunday to get to his Sea Bright home, a day after he got back from work to find his basement "filled up like a swimming pool." But he said the situation around his neighborhood likely would have been much worse if it weren't for new rules requiring homeowners to raise the height of their homes in the wake of Sandy, which devastated the community. He also noticed that many around the community had lined their homes and businesses with sandbags — something he wishes he had done too. "I'm always thinking they are hyping the storm," he said. Seewer reported from Toledo, Ohio. AP journalists Mikella Schuettler in Phoenix and Julie Walker in New York contributed. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Taylor Swift took home the video of the year award as she became the most successful artist in the history of the MTV Video Music Awards on Sunday.
The singer went into the night tied with BeyoncÃ© on 30 wins, and went on to score the night's top award for the visuals for her track The Fate of Ophelia, taken from her 2025 album The Life of a Showgirl.
The original Queen of Pop, Madonna, won artist of the year, best dance and best collaboration alongside Sabrina Carpenter for their dancefloor-filler Bring Your Love, which was the lead single from Madonna's 2026 album Confessions II.
Swift also received the inaugural award for artist director, having written and directed the glitzy and theatrical Ophelia music video herself.
She dedicated her new award to the "ultimate showgirl", saying: "I think we were all very lucky to share this planet with Dolly Parton for a time".
The 36-year-old also debuted the music video for her new song Patient Zero - starring actors Colin Farrell and Dakota Johnson - during the Los Angeles ceremony, hosted by rapper Snoop Dogg.
The dark gothic thriller is her first music video since marrying NFL player Travis Kelce.
The song is one of four new tracks on The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore, which dropped last week.
Female artists awarded
In a ceremony that largely awarded female artists, Madonna went into the night with the most nominations - 13.
And her team also won best cinematography and choreography both for Confessions II, the film.
"Most of you were probably not born when I performed at the very first VMAs 43 years ago," the 68-year-old said after winning artist of the year.
She went on to recall how she had fallen over and exposed her backside, an accident which had threatened to end her fledgling career.
Reflecting on more recent times, she added: "I spent the last year and a half finding myself, believing in myself and really making the music that I wanted to make."
Madonna's performance - her first VMAs show since her infamous onstage kiss with Britney Spears in 2003 - included a duet with Carpenter and an appearance from British Brat star Charli XCX for a rendition of their new song Danceteria (Afterhours).
While accepting the award for best collab, Madonna noted how Carpenter's team had taken five days to respond.
"When five days passed and I still didn't get connected with Sabrina and didn't hear back from her about whether she wanted to do a song with me - five days - I DM'd [direct messaged] her," said the star.
"She answered me back and... within weeks we were in the studio together," she continued. "It was fabulous."
Carpenter, who grimaced slightly at the thought of her team having kept the pop icon waiting, clarified: "My team replies. Just so everybody knows, they do respond to people.
"But I respond faster. So direct line to me is always the best way to get in contact."
Swift, Charli XCX and Lisa from K-pop group Blackpink were among the celebrities walking the blue carpet ahead of the event.
Lisa became the first Asian solo artist to win the best pop category for her song Dream, which featured Japanese actor Kentaro Sakaguchi in its music video.
The Thai rapper-singer fended off competition from some of pop music's biggest names, including Swift, Ariana Grande, Olivia Rodrigo.
Lisa, whose real name is Lalisa Manoba, was visibly moved as she accepted her award. Addressing her fans, known as Lillies, the 29-year-old said she "wouldn't be here without you guys".
British singers Raye and Sienna Spiro, who won best new artist, also performed on the night, where there were tributes to the late Parton and George Michael.
Another Brit, PinkPantheress won best art direction alongside Sweden's Zara Larsson for Stateside.
BTS picked up best group and song of the year for Swim, Olivia Rodrigo's The Cure won best alternative and Nirvana were honoured with the Video Vanguard award.

a622d75dcb4e.text: SpaceX's next-generation Starship rocket successfully reached Earth orbit for the first time Monday morning. Why it matters: The massive, fully-reusable Starship is key to SpaceX's commercial spaceflight ambitions, while NASA is counting on a modified version for use as a lunar lander in its Artemis program. Driving the news: Starship launched from South Texas just before 9 a.m. ET on a planned test flight of about 10 hours. It's set to orbit Earth about six times before splashing down in the Pacific Ocean, west of Chile. As part of the mission, Starship will deploy 26 of the company's new, better-performing Starlink V3 internet satellites. Zoom in: Starship's first-stage Super Heavy booster splashed down in the Gulf of America shortly after launch. SpaceX says this Super Heavy was modified after ice clogging issues interfered with a splashdown attempt on the last test flight. What they're saying: " Flight tests until this point have intentionally flown passively safe suborbital trajectories to maximize public safety while allowing for maximum learning," SpaceX says in a mission summary. "By going to orbit, the next phase of developing Starship to be fully and rapidly reusable can begin." What's next: SpaceX plans to eventually "catch" Starship in the arms of its launch tower — a feat it's accomplished with Super Heavy, but not Starship — but isn't making the attempt this time. Editor's note: This story has been updated with the latest developments.

e0c0368a1b56.text:
The first time I was in Punta San Juan, the desert was flooded with birds. It was 2012, and I was making a short documentary film about the cormorants, pelicans and penguins that made this arid peninsula in southern Peru one of the largest gatherings of seabirds on Earth.
At the time, this 133-acre reserve — a patch of rock and sand jutting into the frigid waters of the Pacific Ocean — was home to more than a quarter million seabirds, including 300,000 Guanay cormorants (Leucocarbo bougainvilliorum) and some 3,000 Humboldt penguins (Spheniscus humboldti).
One of the few species of desert penguin, the Humboldt live along the arid coast of Peru and Chile, where they nest in burrows dug into guano deposits or small cliff caves. Punta San Juan was home to the largest colony in Peru.
By 2025, there were fewer than 500 penguins left. Avian flu had spread through the reserve in 2022 and 2023, crashing seabird populations and spreading to marine mammals such as sea lions and seals. El Niño struck next. The climate pattern is characterized by months of warmer than usual sea surface temperatures in the eastern equatorial Pacific. Those warm waters pushed anchovy — the penguins’ main food source — deeper and farther out to sea. Industrial fishing operations put even more pressure on the surviving animals.
Ecologist Susana Cárdenas-Alayza, who has run the Punta San Juan Program in partnership with Cayetano Heredia University, the Peruvian government and American zoos for more than 20 years, is increasingly alarmed. As a scientist, Cárdenas-Alayza says, she is used to dealing with numbers and controlled variables, “but diseases and climate events escape my control.”
Now, the reserve is facing a new threat: a potential “super” El Niño. Soaring sea surface temperatures are disrupting the cold, fish-rich waters of the Humboldt Current, which flows past the peninsula. When I returned in July, much had changed from my first trip, when streams of penguins lined the cliffs of the reserve. This time I saw only five penguins — and several abandoned nests with cold eggs. When food is scarce, penguins either stop reproducing or leave their nests altogether to search for a more favorable habitat, Cárdenas-Alayza says. They often starve along the way.
The destruction has also been hard on the reserve’s volunteers, who protect the penguins in what Cárdenas-Alayza calls a “living laboratory.” For decades, volunteers from around Peru and the rest of the world have counted birds, recorded their diets and built artificial nests to keep penguin chicks safe. In the summer of 2025, they even launched a “penguin patrol” to safeguard the Humboldts from workers harvesting guano, nitrogen-rich bird droppings essential for agriculture. Wanting to pitch in, the workers built a temporary, half-kilometer-long wall out of sacks of guano to shield the penguins on their daily walk to the sea.
Keeping research going — and morale high — in the emptying ecosystem has been one of the biggest challenges of Cárdenas-Alayza’s career. No one knows how long the current El Niño will last — or when the fish will return.
Nevertheless, Cárdenas-Alayza says she still has hope. Many species in Punta San Juan are philopatric, or loyal to their territory. That means that even when they leave in search of food or other resources, they eventually come back.
Biologist Patricia Majluf, who founded the Punta San Juan Program in 1979, shares one example of resilience: The El Niño event of 1997–98 decimated the reserve’s sea lions and seals. Penguin numbers dropped into the low hundreds. But the animals eventually mounted a remarkable recovery, helped by a major reduction in anchovy fishing quotas in 2006.
Scientists are busy preparing Punta San Juan for the animals’ return. Cárdenas-Alayza briefed incoming members of Peru’s Congress on the situation in July, and she and her fellow researchers are lobbying hard for stricter fishing quotas. They are also championing a new ecosystem restoration strategy, a collaborative framework that engages fishing communities, companies, students and even local chefs to help the reserve’s animals recover.
Back in Punta San Juan, Cárdenas-Alayza’s team is pressuring the government to reinforce a protective concrete wall around the reserve. In the meantime, they are trapping invasive species that prey on young birds, such as foxes and rats. They are also developing AI tools to speed data analysis from remote cameras monitoring breeding among the surviving Humboldt penguins.
As I prepared to leave, Cárdenas-Alayza, Majluf and I shared a meal of chifa, a Peruvian-Chinese cuisine that is a traditional Sunday dinner for Peruvian families. The three of us talked about our experiences teaching and people we had known at the reserve — and Cárdenas-Alayza teased Majluf, saying she was her “conservation mom.” It was at that moment that I realized what kept drawing me back to the reserve. I had come to document the region’s desert penguins, but I had learned so much more: Conservation isn’t just about science; it’s about relationships. At the end of the meal, we all opened our fortune cookies. Cárdenas-Alayza laughed when she saw hers: “Mountains are meant to be climbed.”
Anna Elisa Sotelo’s work on this story was supported by the Pulitzer Center.

Plans for a data centre which would have been built metres from people's homes in a Sydney suburb have been scrapped following intense push-back by campaigners.
The data centre was being developed by Goodman Group, Australia's biggest property company, and would have seen it construct a A$1.2bn (Â£630m; $841m), 90-megawatt facility known as Project Mars in the Lane Cove area.
The company confirmed it was withdrawing its application in a letter to the local planning authority. It follows a concerted opposition against the data centre by local residents and campaigners.
The dispute captures a wider disagreement in Australia over the role of data centres.
With the mainstreaming of generative AI in recent years, there has been a huge swell in demand for data centres, and Australia - with its abundance of clean energy, natural gas reserves, and land - has become a global destination for their construction.
However, while the country's government has been keen to attract investment from global AI companies, there has also been stiff opposition due to the huge demands the centres place on water and energy supplies, and the disruption they cause local communities.
The proposal for Project Mars, which would have been constructed about 20 metres from the nearest house in the suburb of Lane Cove, received 374 submissions during a consultation - with just nine in support of it.
According to local news website In the Cove, this is highest number of submissions ever received for a data centre application, external.
In its letter to New South Wales Department of Planning, Goodman Group said since starting the planning process in March 2025, it had "undertaken extensive technical investigations, stakeholder engagement and community consultation".
"During this time, the policy and regulatory environment for large-scale data centre development has evolved significantly," it said.
It said it had "carefully considered these changes" along with the "views of the local community", and concluded it would not proceed with the development.
The decision by Goodman Group follows an announcement by the New South Wales government last month that it would be introducing a fast-track programme for data centres.
The programme would allow them to be assessed within 75 days, provided they meet requirements around certain standards and fund the additional supply of water and energy.
In a message posted to the Facebook page of Lane Cove Responsible Planning Group, Anthony Roberts, a member of the New South Wales Legislative Assembly representing Lane Cove, said it was "a huge win for the Lane Cove West community".
"This is a common-sense win for our community," he said.
"This victory sends a clear message to other data centre developers. To find suitable locations before putting proposals forward.
"Data centres have an important role to play, but developments of this size and scale need to be appropriately located and planned with the surrounding community in mind."

The Scene
The International Monetary Fundâs forecast for the world economy is increasingly a forecast for AI.
Global growth is tracking at about 3% this year, exactly where it was expected to be 18 months ago, despite two wars, $100 oil, simmering trade battles, and higher borrowing costs. IMF chief Kristalina Georgievaâs explanation: The Middle East conflict is a supply shock dragging growth down, while the AI investment boom is a demand shock pushing it up.
She worries about what happens when one side gives. Stockpiles cushioning the oil shock will run out eventually, and the AI boom is only as durable as investor enthusiasm. Georgieva, who has run the IMF since 2019, points to Amaraâs Law â that we overestimate new technology in the short run and underestimate it in the long run â as a warning that the risks are front-loaded, as investment piles up before widespread adoption brings economic gains to justify it.
The bill is also landing on countries that did nothing to run it up. Emerging economies that spent years tightening their budgets, working their way back into bondholdersâ good graces, are watching rising Treasury yields erase those gains â âthe punishment for somebody elseâs sins,â she said.
Q&A
This interview, conducted onstage at Semaforâs The Next 3 Billion on Sept. 22, has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Liz Hoffman: There are two major wars, oil is at $100, and everyone is worried about asset bubbles. Yet the IMFâs growth forecast for 2026 is 3%, exactly where it was 18 months ago, and the outlook for 2027 has actually improved. How?
Kristalina Georgieva: The negative supply shock from the war in the Middle East pulls the economy down. The positive demand shock from AI is pushing it up. So far, these forces have balanced each other.
The second reason is we once again have demonstrated that there is a lot of creativity in how to deal with problems. You hear a lot of talk about, âoh, cooperation is dead.â But actually, we cooperate because of enlightened self-interest. The United States, Norway, a couple of countries in Africa, have increased oil production very rapidly. Saudi Arabia and the Emirates found ways to bring oil to market through different routes. We have seen the incredible restraint of a large economy like China in going to market to buy oil, using its reserves [instead]. As an economist, I say bravo: We react to market signals. Prices go up, we consume less.
Now, can I give you some bad news? We cannot take this resilience for granted. This energy shock is not over, and nobody can tell you when exactly it will end. What I know is it will get worse before it gets better. Do you like Game of Thrones? Winter is coming. In the Northern Hemisphere, we will use more.
Is that a literal winter, or a metaphorical winter that youâre warning of?
Actually, Iâm warning you. We will see pressure building up. We might see prices of refined products going even further up. That pushes inflation up, and that forces central banks to [raise interest rates]. In normal times, that would not be a giant problem. But these are not normal times, because we have debt levels in advanced economies at historic highs. And when interest rates go up, interest payments go up, and that suffocates the governmentâs ability to do anything, including to help people with the high cost of living. So we should prepare for people being more unhappy in many places, maybe on the street.
Now enters AI. The reason there is so much enthusiasm is because AI companies are profitable. And AI is no [longer] an exciting story only for the United States. You look at the AI supply chain, and you see countries in Asia plugged into it, like Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore.
Imagine what would happen if our enthusiasm cools off and money pulls out from the massive investments that have been made. Then we can be in real trouble. So be careful. Keep your eyes open and listen to the IMF.
Is the flip side of that AI supply chain thatâs been benefiting countries in Asia that weâve just exported the risk and globalized what might otherwise just be a Silicon Valley bubble?
Yes. It also stabilizes it, because then you have more production that may not be so bubbly. But yes, it makes it a global phenomenon.
I think in the long run, we will be amazed at what has been done as a result of this technology. But if we donât come to our senses to have some ethical foundation and rules, we might not be able to see these benefits coming. I was going to say we may not be able to live long enough, but thatâs a little too extreme.
AI is often pitched as an equalizer for developing nations. But it requires a lot of limited resources â power, compute â and there are a lot of languages in the world that the current models donât serve well. How do you think about that?
There is, of course, a tremendous opportunity for leapfrogging for developing countries, and also for plugging themselves into the value chain. There is also tremendous risk that the accordion of inequality would open even wider. In developing countries, prerequisites like access to electricity, access to the internet, are just not there. And you canât really take advantage of AI without them.
Do you worry that at the company level, at the economy level, people are saying, âwith AI we can grow our way out of this holeâ and that itâs allowing a little bit of financial indiscipline to come in?
Please donât do that [laughs]. Yes, AI is likely to deliver significant productivity gains. But itâs not going to happen overnight and in the meanwhile, the story of the last years is: shock, governments borrow, spend, then they do nothing to reduce [spending]. So we are on this staircase, not to heaven. I think we are not really seriously assessing the implications of this problem in a world of interest rates going up. Please donât spend money you donât have.
If investors can get US government debt at almost 5% today, is that crowding out the ability of emerging economies to borrow?
Ma

7df28483ae12.text:
Waelâs view
Saudi Arabiaâs stock market has problems that cannot be solved simply by listing more companies. It now has a regulator who has lived with the marketâs shortcomings, both as an investor and a government official.
Tadawul is already big, with a market value of about 9.30 trillion riyals ($2.48 trillion) in the week ended Sept. 24. But its benchmark index had its steepest annual decline in a decade last year, falling 12.8% in 2025 despite relative stability in the region and rapid growth in the kingdomâs non-oil economy. The index closed at 10,681.84 on Sept. 27. The marketâs size masks a bourse that lacks depth, liquidity, and trust.
That is the central task facing Mazen Al-Sudairi, appointed last month as chairman of the Capital Market Authority. Al-Sudairi spent years at Al Rajhi Capital before moving into government, where he holds an external seat on Public Investment Fundâs investment committee, among other positions. That gives him an understanding of how the kingdom evaluates assets it plans to bring to public markets.
Among Al-Sudairiâs biggest challenges is bridging the gap between the stock market and the broader economy. Tadawul, while the regionâs largest exchange, remains dominated by a few sectors and has failed to capture many of the private businesses benefiting from the kingdomâs Vision 2030 transformation. As CMA chairman, Al-Sudairi reports to the prime minister, effectively Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, giving him the institutional weight to make bold decisions.
Two recent circulars suggest he is using the most immediate levers at his disposal.
On Sept. 8, the CMA capped public money-market fundsâ foreign investments at 5% of net assets. The funds, which function as a quasi-deposit product, are a major home for short-term corporate and individual liquidity. The measure should redirect more of that money into domestic instruments, although its success will depend on whether the products offer competitive returns.
Nine days later, the CMA reminded listed companies that board pay must be clearly linked to individual and corporate performance. Companies whose policies fall short must correct them. The circular named no company, but the warning suggests the regulator intends to scrutinize governance more closely.
The move followed a June paper from the PIF-affiliated Corporate Governance Center, which studied board pay at 345 listed companies and more than 2,400 directors. It found that only 10% of companies offer variable board compensation, while government-linked firms pay more than double the market average, even after accounting for size and sector. The paper recommended that companies explain why their pay arrangements are appropriate rather than merely disclose the figures. The CMAâs circular follows the centerâs recommendation.
Together, the CMAâs measures could be seen as quick wins, and neither required new legislation or getting a huge listing to trade. But neither addresses Tadawulâs deeper problems.
Saudi Arabian stocks peaked in 2006 and have yet to recover. Investors have compelling alternatives abroad, including US technology stocks, global funds, larger free floats, and better hedging tools. Capping money-market fundsâ foreign exposure may force managers to redirect some capital, but it doesnât make Saudi stocks more attractive.
The IPO problem cuts deeper. The CMAâs 2025 annual report shows that 39 public equity offerings raised 18.65 billion riyals ($4.97 billion), up 41% from 2024. Yet approved offering and registration applications fell to 36 from 60. Semafor has reported that the CMA is examining how banks priced and allocated recent IPOs after several listings fell below their offer prices.
Retail investors can accept volatility. What they struggle to accept is the sense that an IPO was structured chiefly to maximize proceeds for the sellers, leaving the public with the downside. In some recent offerings, most or all of the shares were sold by existing shareholders rather than issued by the company to grow the business.
Founders, heirs, and venture firms have every right to monetize. But Al-Sudairi must decide what Tadawulâs primary function should be: financing the next phase of corporate growth, or providing an exit for those who financed the last one.
The market will always be a mix of both, and one type of company embodies this dichotomy: family businesses. They account for almost 95% of Saudi establishments and employ 57% of private-sector workers. Bringing even a fraction to market would diversify Tadawul more meaningfully than another state-backed mega-listing. But families need governance structures that protect outside shareholders without leaving founders fearful of losing control.
Getting those companies onto Tadawul is only part of Al-Sudairiâs mission to make the market easier to trade, harder to misprice, and more useful to companies seeking capital. Two circulars are a start, and success will be measured by whether companies list in Saudi Arabia to build rather than whether their owners come simply to leave.
Wael Mahdi is an independent commentator specializing in OPEC and Saudi Arabiaâs economy, and co-author of OPEC in a Shale Oil World: Where to Next?
Notable
- Saudi Arabiaâs stock market regulator is investigating the poor performance of recent IPOs, including looking into the advice given by investment banks as it tries to kickstart new listings, Semafor reported.
